keeping-flowers-upright-4.solvingTip: Try the clue about the narrow place where you walk. Its crossing letters can help with the actions you take to set the plant tag upright.

clues.NAME: What a tag tells you to call a plant
clues.SET: Put a plant tag in its place

notes.LABEL: A plant label faces the walkway so you can read it from outside the bed.
notes.STRAIGHT: A label can stand straight even if its top edge curves.
notes.PRESS: Press describes a steady downward push as the tag goes back into the soil.

garden-repairs-and-labels-2.solvingTip: Start with the tool whose writing can be erased. Then look at the clues for the words that go on a plant tag.

clues.LABEL: Tag that tells you which plant is growing
clues.DATE: Day and month you might record when planting
clues.LETTER: Alphabet character scratched on a plant tag

notes.LABEL: A plant label can carry a name or tell you when that row was planted.
notes.PENCIL: The point on a pencil leaves erasable marks on paper.
notes.MARKER: A marker can be the sign itself. In this garden it stands beside the plant it identifies.

tending-vegetable-rows-3.solvingTip: Start with the three-letter answers for a familiar color and the highest part. Those letters can help you name the part of the root you see at ground level.

clues.SHOULDER: Part of a round root that widens just below its leaves
clues.ROOT: Part of a plant that grows down into the ground
clues.SOIL: Loose ground in a garden bed

notes.RADISH: The round part of a garden radish is usually its root. Its leaves grow above it.
notes.ROOT: Some roots store food for the plant. The crisp part of a radish is one example.
notes.SHOULDER: Gardeners use shoulder for the upper part of a root vegetable where it starts to widen.

spring-at-the-market-4.focus: This market bunch has roots and leafy tops. The clues follow it from the stall to the kitchen.
spring-at-the-market-4.solvingTip: Start with the two color clues. One names the color of the tops, and the other can describe the skin of the vegetable.

clues.CRUNCH: Sound you hear when you bite a crisp radish
clues.RINSE: Wash the bunch under clean running water
clues.SLICE: One thin round cut from a radish
clues.GREEN: Color of the radish's leafy tops
clues.SPRING: Cool season when early radishes can be harvested

notes.SLICE: Cutting a radish across the root gives small round slices. The red skin makes a bright rim around the pale center.
notes.GREEN: Green here describes the leafy tops of the radish. The round part below them is the root, which can have red skin and a pale middle.
notes.SPRING: Radishes grow well in cool weather and can be one of the first roots pulled in spring. Leaving the tops attached makes it easy to hold the bunch under running water.

harvest-basket-details-4.solvingTip: Try the clue for the plant part just above the pepper. Then look for a short word that names the cut made there.

clues.BASKET: Woven container for carrying vegetables from the garden
clues.PEPPER: Garden vegetable that can be a sweet bell or a hot chili
clues.STEM: Part joining a pepper to the plant

notes.SHEARS: Garden shears have two blades that cut as the handles close.
notes.PEPPER: Sweet bell peppers and hot chili peppers both grow attached by a stem.
notes.SNIP: A snip is one short, quick cut of the blades.

gardens-after-cold-2.solvingTip: Start with the season after winter. The clue about how the stalk tastes can help you identify the plant used in pies.

clues.RHUBARB: Plant with tart stalks often baked in pies
clues.FIRM: Holding its shape when gently pressed

notes.RHUBARB: Rhubarb stalks can be red or green. The tart stalk is the part used in pies.
notes.STALK: The stalk is the long part below one of the broad leaves.
notes.RED: The clue asks for a color. Rhubarb stalks can show that color even before they are cut.

small-tools-at-a-paper-desk.solvingTip: Start with the short clues for the writing tool and the liquid it leaves. Then look for the word for taking that liquid up with paper.

clues.LEDGER: Book for keeping track of money coming in and going out
clues.BLOT: Soak up extra ink by touching it with dry paper

notes.BLOT: Blotting paper takes up wet ink when it touches the page. Sliding the paper can smear the line.
notes.INK: Ink can stay wet briefly after writing, especially when a pen leaves a heavy line.
notes.LEDGER: A ledger keeps a record of amounts paid or received, often in separate columns.

everyday-materials-2.solvingTip: Start with the writing tool whose marks can be erased. Then sort the paper clues by whether they describe one piece or a stack joined at the edge.

clues.PAGE: One side of a sheet in a notebook, often numbered

everyday-moments-with-paper-2.solvingTip: Look for the short clue about using a cloth. Then work toward the word for the see-through holder that protects the directions.

clues.COUNTER: Kitchen work surface beside a mixing bowl
clues.POCKET: Sleeve that you slide a paper recipe into
clues.COVER: Layer that protects a page from splashes

notes.POCKET: A clear pocket has an opening along one edge so the paper can slide in and out.
notes.RECIPE: A recipe pairs an ingredient list with directions you can follow in order.
notes.CLEAR: A clear sleeve lets you read the paper through it while you work.

gift-paper-folds-3.solvingTip: Try the short clue about putting a crease in paper. Then look for the words tied to the stiff paper and the directions written on it.

clues.COUNTER: Flat kitchen work surface where a recipe card can sit
clues.MARK: Put a short line or other sign on the recipe card

notes.RECIPE: A recipe card keeps both the ingredient list and the steps close at hand.
notes.CARD: Heavier paper can support itself when it has a crease.
notes.FOLD: The fold gives the card two sides that can rest on the counter like a small tent.

listening-with-old-equipment-2.solvingTip: Begin with a side of the cabinet you can point to. Use the crossings to find the name of the cover on that side.

clues.GRILLE: Cover with holes that lets sound out of a speaker
clues.COVER: Part placed over another part to protect it
clues.RATTLE: Make a quick series of knocks when shaken

notes.GRILLE: A speaker grille protects the parts behind it and has openings so sound can pass through.
notes.RATTLE: A loose cover can knock against its frame even when the speaker is switched off.
notes.LOOSE: A part is loose when it has enough play to move in its fitting.

sounds-of-the-recording-room-3.solvingTip: Think about two things you hear while a song plays. One clue describes brief popping sounds. Another names the control that makes the audio louder or softer.

clues.SPEAKER: Device that plays the sound from a stereo
clues.MUSIC: What you hear when a recorded song plays
clues.CORD: Flexible cable running to a piece of sound equipment
clues.TEST: Check whether the sound comes through clearly
clues.WIRE: Thin strand of metal that carries an electrical signal
clues.VOLUME: How loud the sound coming from the speaker is

notes.SPEAKER: A speaker turns an electrical signal from sound equipment into sound you can hear.
notes.CRACKLE: Crackle is a series of brief pops you might hear through the music.
notes.WIRE: The metal inside a wire carries the signal. A loose connection can interrupt it.

neighbors-and-small-kindnesses-4.solvingTip: Start with the two opposite directions a neighbor might give. Then use the crossings to pick out the landmarks along the way.

clues.STORE: Shop a neighbor might use as a landmark
clues.BLOCK: Stretch of a street between two corners

notes.CORNER: A corner gives both people a place to picture where two streets meet.
notes.POINT: A person can point toward a landmark while saying its name.
notes.TURN: A turn tells the visitor where to stop going straight and change direction.

welcoming-a-new-neighbor.solvingTip: Start with the short clue about moving on foot. Then look for the drawing that shows which streets to take to the shop.

clues.CORNER: Place where two streets meet on the drawing
clues.STORE: Place to buy food or other goods
clues.NEAR: Close enough for a short walk

notes.MAP: A small map can show just the streets between a home and a shop.
notes.GROCERY: A grocery can be the shop itself, while groceries are the goods you bring home.
notes.SKETCH: A quick sketch can use a few street lines and a mark for the shop.

useful-home-repairs-5.focus: Picture a chair being pulled out from a table. This puzzle follows the foot of one leg from bare wood to a small floor protector.
useful-home-repairs-5.solvingTip: Start with the three-letter clue for what supports a chair. Then try the clues for the soft piece that goes under it and the tool that trims it.

clues.STICK: Stay attached to a chair leg

notes.SCISSORS: Scissors can trim a pad to fit the bottom of the chair leg.
notes.CHAIR: A single chair may need a separate protector under each leg.
notes.TABLE: A chair pad protects the floor as the chair is pulled out from a table.

visits-and-welcome.solvingTip: Follow the clue about the narrow way through a room. Then look for the name of the walking aid that needs a place of its own.

clues.CORNER: Place where two walls meet beside an entrance
clues.ENTRY: Place where someone comes into a home
clues.TIP: Bottom end of a cane that touches the floor

notes.CANE: A cane has a part to hold at the top and a tip that meets the floor.
notes.STAND: A stand gives a visitor a place to put a cane where the handle stays within reach.
notes.HANDLE: The handle is the part a visitor reaches for when getting up to leave.

pantry-packets-and-labels-2.solvingTip: Start with the short action that shakes away loose flour. Then look for the word for an even top and the tool you tapped.

clues.POWDER: Fine dry particles, such as ground flour
clues.SHELF: Flat board that holds things in a pantry
clues.SCOOP: Small utensil with a bowl and handle for moving flour
clues.TIN: Metal container that can hold flour and its scoop

notes.SCOOP: A scoop moves flour a little at a time. Its handle keeps your hand above the flour.
notes.LEVEL: A level scoop has an even top up to its edge. A heaped scoop rises above it.
notes.TAP: A light tap is a small knock. Here it shakes flour loose from the scoop.

pantry-choices-5.solvingTip: Try the clue for what the flour comes in. Then look for the short answer for the tool that measures a portion of it.

clues.MEASURE: Find out how much flour you have in the cup
clues.CUP: Kitchen measure for a portion of flour

comfort-food-from-the-oven.solvingTip: Begin with the three-letter action you do with a spoon as the sauce cooks. Then look for how the sauce changes when it becomes less runny.

notes.KERNEL: Each kernel is one seed. A cob holds many of them in rows.
notes.SAUCE: The sauce coats the kernels and makes the corn easy to serve by the spoonful.
notes.MILK: Milk can be part of the liquid used to make the creamy sauce.

vegetable-side-dishes-5.focus: Picture kernels coming off a cooked ear of corn. The puzzle follows them from the cob to a simple side dish.
vegetable-side-dishes-5.solvingTip: Start with the short clue about what is left once the kernels come off. Then find the spread that melts on the hot corn.

clues.KERNEL: One grain in a row on an ear of corn
clues.SIDE: Dish you serve alongside the main course
clues.SWEET: Sugary in taste, as some buttered corn can be
clues.SPOON: Curved utensil used to serve loose corn kernels

notes.SWEET: Sweet is the taste of the corn kernels. Butter and a pinch of salt add other flavors when the kernels are served warm.
notes.SPOON: Loose corn kernels can roll off a flat utensil. The curved bowl of a serving spoon holds several of them together as you lift a portion.
notes.BUTTER: Once the warm kernels are cut from the cob, toss them with a little butter. It can melt around each loose kernel.

small-baking-checks-2.solvingTip: Start with the short clue for the baking container. Then look for the words that tell what you do with the paper once the batch has cooled.

clues.LEVEL: Even from one side of the pan to the other
clues.PAPER: Baking liner that you can lift when the batch is cool
clues.COOL: Lose heat after coming out of the oven
clues.LIFT: Raise the cooled batch out of the pan

notes.ENDS: Extra paper above two sides gives the baker somewhere to hold the liner.
notes.LIFT: The paper helps bring the cooled batch out in one piece before it is cut.
notes.BARS: Bar cookies bake together in a pan and are cut into pieces after baking.

kitchen-small-jobs-5.solvingTip: Think of the empty baking pan. Start with the clue for the place where two edges meet, then find the action that helps the paper fit there.

clues.PAPER: Thin material placed between the baking mixture and the pan
clues.LIFT: Raise an edge of the liner to adjust it

sounds-heard-together-3.solvingTip: Think of a familiar song. Try the clue for the part whose words change, then the clue for the part the singers know will repeat.

clues.VOICE: Sound you make when you speak or sing
clues.LOUDER: Easier to hear because the sound is stronger

notes.CHORUS: The chorus is the part many songs repeat with the same words.
notes.VERSE: One verse can use the same tune as another while telling a different part of the story.
notes.LOUDER: Singers can increase the volume together as they reach the chorus.

singalong-preparations.solvingTip: Picture someone touching the piano once so everyone can hear where to begin. Try the clues for what the player presses and what the singers hear.

clues.VOICE: Sound made by a singer's vocal cords
clues.HIGH: Toward the top of the range a singer can reach

night-outdoors-3.focus: A cricket has strong back legs and can disappear into the lawn with a quick leap.
night-outdoors-3.solvingTip: Start with the action that sends the insect off the ground. Then use the body-part clues to picture how it moves.

clues.CHIRP: Make a short, high sound as a cricket does
clues.WING: Part of an insect's body used for flight
clues.NIGHT: Time after dark when cricket calls may be heard
clues.GRASS: Low plants a cricket may hide among beside a porch

notes.NIGHT: A cricket's chirp can be easier to notice at night when the porch and yard grow quiet. The sound comes from rubbing parts of its wings together.
notes.GRASS: Grass at the porch edge can hide a cricket even while it chirps. The sound can seem to move when the insect jumps to another spot.
notes.INSECT: A cricket's hind legs are longer than its other legs. That is the pair it uses to make the jumps in this scene.

easy-games-with-a-table-4.solvingTip: Start at the first tile in your mind. Try the short word for the little push that makes it lean toward the next one.

clues.DOMINO: Small rectangular game piece with two marked halves
clues.BLOCK: Solid piece small enough to set on its end
clues.TILE: Flat piece that can stand on edge in the row
clues.PLAY: Have fun with a game or toy

notes.DOMINO: A domino can stand on its narrow end even though it usually lies flat during a game.
notes.UPRIGHT: Upright pieces have enough height to reach the next piece as they fall.
notes.TIP: Here tip means give the first tile a small push so it tilts.

quiet-table-hobbies-5.focus: The next tile can join the line when the marked end fits the end already showing.
quiet-table-hobbies-5.solvingTip: Try the clue for a single round mark on a tile. Then look for what players call a piece with the same count at both ends.

clues.LINE: Row of tiles laid end to end
clues.WHITE: Color of fresh snow or some domino tiles

notes.WHITE: Some sets use white tiles with dark dots. Others reverse the colors.
notes.LINE: In this game, the line is the row of tiles that grows as players add matching ends.

garden-harvest-baskets.solvingTip: Start with the color of the leafy tops. Then picture what you might carry the carrots in after pulling them.

clues.ORANGE: Color of most carrots sold at the market
clues.FORK: Utensil with prongs you might use to eat carrots at supper

notes.GREEN: Most carrot tops are green. You can often see them before pulling the root from the ground.
notes.BASKET: A shallow basket can hold the long carrots across its base. They can go in straight from the row and be rinsed at the sink afterward.
notes.CARROT: A carrot root can break if the soil grips it tightly. Loosening the soil beside the row gives the root room to come out whole.

garden-from-the-beginning-3.solvingTip: Picture the new container from top to bottom. Try the clues for its upper edge and the small opening where extra water escapes.

clues.WATER: What you pour into the soil around a dry seedling
clues.LIFT: Raise the seedling gently out of its old pot
clues.HOLE: Opening at the bottom of a pot where extra water can escape
clues.ROOT: Thin underground part that can be lifted with a seedling

notes.WATER: Water that the soil cannot hold can leave through the opening in the bottom of the pot.
notes.SOIL: Moving a seedling with some soil around its roots helps keep the roots together.
notes.ROOT: Seedling roots can be fine and easy to pull apart. Lifting the plant from below keeps more of those fine roots together during the move.

garden-evening-chores-2.solvingTip: Begin with the tool you would use to gather dirt from the floor. Then find the part that lets the shed door swing.

clues.LATCH: Small fastening that holds the shed door shut
clues.DUST: Fine dirt that settles on a shed shelf
clues.DOOR: Movable panel that opens so you can enter a shed
clues.SHED: Small building where a rake is stored

notes.SHELF: A shelf keeps small items off the floor where the boots go. Long tools can hang on hooks nearby, leaving the shelf clear for smaller supplies.
notes.DOOR: The shed door swings out of the way while you sweep the entrance. Once the tools are put away, its latch can hold it closed again.
notes.SHED: The shed gives the rake and broom a place out of the weather. Clear the doorway first so you can carry the long tools inside without catching them on the door.

memories-of-main-street-4.solvingTip: Try the short word for what the delivery rider pedals. Then think about the stops the rider makes before breakfast.

clues.PAPER: Material the morning news is printed on
clues.FOLD: Bend one half of the newspaper over the other
clues.PORCH: Front entry platform where a newspaper can be delivered
clues.ROUTE: Course a newspaper carrier follows from house to house

notes.PAPER: Folding the printed paper makes a large newspaper easier to carry on a delivery route.
notes.PORCH: A newspaper left on the porch can be picked up at the door. Setting it back from the steps keeps it farther from the rain.
notes.ROUTE: A paper route is the set of homes where the carrier delivers newspapers. Going in the same order each morning can make it easier to remember every stop.

memories-of-home-entertainment-4.solvingTip: Start with the person who introduces the songs. Then try the clues about choosing the broadcast and asking for a favorite song.

clues.LISTENER: Person who tunes in to the program
clues.STATION: Broadcaster you can tune in to on the radio
clues.DIAL: Numbered control used to tune an old radio

notes.LETTER: A listener could mail a letter to ask the host to play a favorite song.
notes.RADIO: On older radios, turning the dial lets you move between broadcasts.
notes.VOICE: A radio host's voice connects one song to the next. It may tell you who made the request or what record you are about to hear.

saved-messages.solvingTip: Try the short clue for a row of print. Picture following that row from the name on the left to the digits you need to call.

clues.THICK: Having many pages, as a big phone book does
clues.PAGES: Numbered sides you turn through in a phone book

notes.SURNAME: A surname is a family name. Residential phone books often list it before the given name.
notes.ALPHABET: Names are arranged from A to Z. If two names begin with the same letter, the following letters determine their order.
notes.NUMBER: The telephone number usually appears on the same line as the household's name.

errands-on-main-street-2.solvingTip: Imagine the counter at the post office. Start with what the clerk uses to weigh a letter, then try the clue for what covers the cost of mailing it.

clues.CLERK: Worker who helps you at the post office counter
clues.SEAL: Close the flap securely before mailing
clues.CODE: ZIP ___ written after the state on a mailing address

notes.ENVELOPE: At the post office, the envelope and everything inside it are weighed together. An extra page can change how much postage the letter needs.
notes.LETTER: A mailed letter is the message you want someone to read. It goes inside the envelope, where the writing stays covered during delivery.
notes.ADDRESS: Put the destination address where the post office can read it on the front of the envelope. The smaller return address can go in the upper left corner.

visits-and-gatherings.solvingTip: Start with the small thing you drink from. Then picture what goes underneath it and what carries it to the table.

clues.SAUCER: Small dish that goes under a cup
clues.SUGAR: Sweet crystals you might stir into coffee

notes.CHAIR: A chair at the table gives a guest a place to sit while the coffee is poured.
notes.SUGAR: Granulated sugar is easy to spoon into a cup and dissolves when stirred into hot coffee.
notes.COFFEE: Coffee can be poured into each cup at the table. A saucer gives the guest a place to set the cup and a spoon between sips.

shopping-and-returning.solvingTip: Start with the walkway between store shelves. At the checkout, think about the words for the offer's last day and the money you keep.

clues.SIZE: How big the package is, as listed in the offer

notes.COUPON: A paper coupon may apply only to a certain brand or package size.
notes.CASHIER: The cashier applies the discount at the register when the purchase meets the offer terms.
notes.EXPIRES: After the date printed on the offer, the discount is no longer valid.

garden-harvest-baskets-2.solvingTip: Begin with the color seen on many ripe tomatoes. Then distinguish the support around a plant from the upright support beside it.

clues.TOMATO: Juicy garden fruit often sliced for a sandwich
clues.FRUIT: Part of a plant that holds its seeds
clues.SLICE: One flat piece cut from a tomato

notes.FRUIT: A tomato develops from a flower and contains the plant's seeds, so it is a fruit in gardening terms.
notes.SLICE: A slice is a piece cut across the tomato. Cutting across its widest part usually gives a broad piece that shows several seed pockets.
notes.TOMATO: A ripe tomato can be twisted gently away from its stem when you pick it. The stake or cage still supports the vine and any fruit left on it.

street-sights-remembered-2.solvingTip: Start with the small piece of money that opens the rack. Then picture the narrow opening where you put it.

clues.SLOT: Narrow opening that takes a coin
clues.LIFT: Raise the rack's front panel to reach the paper

notes.NEWSPAPER: A sidewalk rack could hold a stack of the same day's edition for people passing by.
notes.COIN: Older newspaper racks often opened after a customer put in the posted amount.
notes.SLOT: The opening is sized for coins. It leads into the locked part of the rack that holds the money.

family-photos-and-film-4.solvingTip: Imagine attaching a picture to an album page. Start with the clue for sticky material, then try the clue for the part of the picture that has ripped.

clues.SLIP: Slide a corner of the picture into its little holder
clues.HOLD: Keep the picture in place on the page

notes.PHOTO: A photo corner can hold a print against the album page with the glue on the holder instead of on the picture.
notes.TORN: A torn corner may have lost some paper, so a small holder works best when it can still catch the remaining edge.
notes.CORNER: A corner is where two edges of the picture meet. An album holder fits over that point.

bakers-specialties-2.solvingTip: Try the clue for the opening in the middle. Then picture which words describe the bagel before it goes in the oven and which describe it at breakfast.

eating-at-the-diner-5.solvingTip: Start with what the server brings the waffle on. Then think of the small spaces where the berry juice settles.

clues.WAFFLE: Breakfast food with a grid of small squares
clues.IRON: Hinged cooking tool that makes a waffle's grid
clues.POUR: Tip the batter from a bowl so it flows into the waffle maker
clues.SPOON: Utensil that lifts berries and their juice together

notes.WAFFLE: The hot plates of a waffle iron shape the squares on both sides as the batter cooks.
notes.BERRIES: Juice from cooked or crushed berries can collect in the small hollows.
notes.POCKETS: The pockets are the little spaces between the raised lines on the waffle.

garden-protection-5.solvingTip: Start with the clue for the upright support. Then look for the part that opens so you can walk into the larger growing area.

clues.BED: One patch of soil set aside for growing plants
clues.GARDEN: Place containing the patches where you grow vegetables

listening-with-old-equipment-5.solvingTip: Start with the tool you can sharpen. Then look for the center part the tool turns and what winds back onto the reel.

clues.HUB: Center part of a reel that the pencil turns
clues.PENCIL: Writing tool with a point you can sharpen
clues.TAPE: Thin strip that holds the cassette's recorded sound

comfort-food-from-the-oven-3.solvingTip: Try the three-letter clue for what holds the dessert in the oven. Then think of the fruits used for cider and the grains in the topping.

clues.APPLES: Fruits often pressed to make cider

keeping-food-fresh-4.solvingTip: Start with the clue for the place where the cake sits. Then look for the rounded cover you raise before cutting a piece.

clues.LIFT: Raise the cake's glass cover to take a piece
clues.CRUMB: Tiny bit that breaks off when cake is cut

notes.PLATE: Here the plate is the flat surface holding the cake. The dome is the separate cover that lifts away so you can cut a slice.
notes.SWEET: Icing adds a sweet outer layer to the cake. The crumb is the soft inside that you see when you lift out a slice.
notes.SLICE: For a round cake, two cuts from the middle to the edge make a wedge-shaped slice. The word slice can name that serving even if it has a curved edge.

garden-fruit-variety-4.solvingTip: Start with the short clue for what catches the falling fruit. Then use its crossings to name the material with small openings.

clues.NET: What you set under the tree to catch the cherries
clues.SPREAD: Open out the mesh so it covers more ground
clues.MESH: Open-weave material that lets rain pass through

notes.MESH: Mesh has small openings. They let rain pass through the net while larger cherries stay on top.

flower-display-details.solvingTip: Start with the color you might see in a small rose. Then look for the narrow piece of fabric that holds the flower against the cloth.

clues.SET: Put in place, as a flower tucked under a ribbon

town-events-behind-scenes-3.solvingTip: Start with the clue for what you hear when someone speaks. Then look for the device at the front that helps people in the back hear it.

clues.TEST: Try the microphone to see if people in the back can hear
clues.VOLUME: How loud the voice sounds through the microphone

stairs-and-hallway.solvingTip: Start with what you put under the floor covering to steady it. Then look for the clue about what the covering does if it moves underfoot.

clues.SLIP: Move out of place under someone's foot
clues.RUG: Floor covering that lies on the landing

everyday-kitchen-repairs.solvingTip: Try the clue for how you open the drawer. Then look for words about the parts it moves along when it works smoothly.

clues.SLIDE: Move smoothly along a cabinet track
clues.RUB: Move against the side of the cabinet as the drawer slides

sorting-and-donating-5.solvingTip: Start with what the jacket hangs from. Then look for the words that tell why the jacket and trousers belong together.

clues.SET: Group of matching pieces kept together
clues.SUIT: Matching jacket and trousers worn together

fabric-on-the-table.solvingTip: Try naming the part of the pan you hold when you lift it. The longer words describe what fits over it and how that cover is sewn.

clues.SLIP: Slide the cloth cover onto the pan handle

gift-paper-folds-4.solvingTip: Picture a note tucked into a roll. Start with the clue for what ties it closed, then try the words for what's inside.

clues.SLIP: Small piece of paper for a short note
clues.CURL: Bend into a curved shape, as rolled paper does

gift-paper-folds-5.solvingTip: Start with the clue for the part that folds over the opening. Then think of how the bookmark moves into the envelope.

handwork-fixing-keepsakes-3.solvingTip: Start with the clue for the picture you want to keep. Then look for what happened to the old holder and what the new one looks like.

clues.SLIP: Move out of a pocket through a tear
clues.POCKET: Small clear holder for a photo in an album
clues.PRINT: Photograph on paper that slips into an album

handwork-fixing-keepsakes-4.solvingTip: Find what hangs on the wall and the small part that holds it there. Then think about what you adjust when one side is too low.

clues.WIRE: Thin metal strand stretched across the back of the frame

old-shop-tools-3.solvingTip: Think about the papers a clerk collects during the day. Start with the clue for what the customer gets after paying.

clues.SLIP: Small piece of paper from a sale
clues.SPIKE: Pointed metal rod that holds receipts in a stack

notes.SPIKE: The spike goes through one end of each receipt. The stack stays in order as the clerk adds slips and can be lifted off together at the end of the day.

old-shop-tools-5.solvingTip: Start with the short clue for what holds the item being weighed. Then look for the words about moving the weight until both sides are even.

clues.SLIDE: Move smoothly along the beam, as the weight does
clues.LEVEL: Same height at both ends, like a balanced scale beam

street-sights-remembered-4.solvingTip: Start with something the rider turns or pushes to move the bicycle. Then find the container at the front that holds the parcel.

notes.SAND: Damp sand near the water packs together more easily than the dry sand farther up the beach. A crab can leave little tracks across that firm surface.

errands-on-main-street-5.solvingTip: Start with the paper you show to collect your clothes. Then look for what the cleaned clothes hang from and what the worker checks on the paper.

breakfast-from-the-stove-3.solvingTip: Start with what you use to eat the warm cereal. Then try the short clue for its grain and either of the two sweet toppings.

clues.BOWL: Deep dish for serving a helping of oatmeal

clues.PAPER: Material a puzzle grid can be printed on

notes.LETTER: Each square holds a single letter. Neighboring letters form a word when you follow the right line.
notes.PAPER: A paper grid lets you mark each word in place as you find it. A pencil makes it easier to erase a line if the letters run the wrong way.
notes.PENCIL: A pencil is useful for marking a word you have found and crossing it off the list. A light line through the letters keeps them readable if another word crosses there.

quiet-table-hobbies-4.solvingTip: Try the clue for the whole pack you lay out. Then look at the colors and shapes of the symbols on individual cards.

notes.DECK: A standard deck has 52 cards divided among four suits.

songs-with-everyday-words-2.solvingTip: Start with what the batter holds and what the pitcher throws. Then look for the short word for cheering, as the song asks fans to do.

clues.FIELD: Ground where baseball players run and catch the ball
clues.BALL: Small round object a pitcher throws toward the batter
clues.BAT: Club a baseball player swings to hit the ball
clues.GAME: Ballpark contest cheered on by fans

notes.FIELD: The ball field includes the infield around the bases and the outfield beyond it.
notes.GAME: In the song title, the game is a baseball game. Fans may root for the home team, which bats in the bottom half of an inning.

animals-on-the-farm-2.solvingTip: Start with the short name of the mother or the young animal. Then find the part of the boundary that swings open.

clues.HOOF: Hard covering on the end of a calf's foot
clues.COW: Farm animal that is the mother of a calf
clues.FENCE: Farm barrier that can enclose a cow and calf

notes.FIELD: A farm field is an open piece of land. Some fields grow crops and others give cattle space to graze.
notes.FENCE: The farm fence keeps the cow and calf in the same enclosed area. The gate is where the farmer can enter to bring hay or feed.
notes.GATE: The gate can be opened to bring something into the farmyard. Closing it again keeps the calf and its mother together inside the fence.

bible-beginnings-3.solvingTip: Start with the name of the man who builds the vessel. Then look for what it is made from and the number of animals that make up a matching group.

clues.WATER: Liquid that covers normally dry land in a flood
clues.BOAT: Vessel that travels or floats on water
clues.PAIR: Group of two animals that go together in the story
clues.FAMILY: Group of relatives who entered the ark with Noah

notes.WATER: In the story, the flood covers the land, and Noah's vessel floats as the water rises.
notes.FAMILY: In Genesis, Noah's family goes into the ark with him. The account includes his wife, his sons, and his sons' wives.
notes.BIRD: In Genesis, birds are among the creatures brought into the ark. Later in the flood story, Noah sends out a raven and a dove.

taking-care-of-small-supplies-3.solvingTip: Start with the shallow holder that goes under the bottles. Then find what splits it into spaces and the word for how the bottles stand.

clues.GROUP: Small set of bottles kept together in one part of the tray

breakfast-on-the-griddle-3.solvingTip: Start with the three-letter clue for the part that comes down over the batter. Then try the clue for the whole cooking tool.

notes.BATTER: Waffle batter needs to flow into the pattern on the iron. A dough, like cookie dough, is usually stiff enough to hold its shape.
notes.IRON: The word iron names the whole appliance here. Its two hot plates cook both sides of the waffle at the same time.

clues.LID: Hinged part you lift to check the waffle
clues.TOP: Upper surface of the cooked waffle
clues.HEAT: Warmth the hot plates give the mixture

cookie-tins-2.solvingTip: Start with the clue for the dried grape. Its crossing letters can help you name the mixture that goes into the oven.

clues.DOUGH: Thick unbaked cookie mixture you can scoop
clues.OVEN: Kitchen appliance that bakes the cookies
clues.RACK: Wire frame that lets cookies cool on both sides
clues.CINNAMON: Brown spice that often flavors oatmeal raisin cookies

notes.FLOUR: Flour mixes into the dough, while the oats can stay visible as flakes. Those two ingredients have different jobs in an oatmeal cookie.
notes.CINNAMON: Ground cinnamon can be mixed with the flour so it spreads through the cookie dough. You can taste the spice even in a bite with no raisin.
notes.DOUGH: Oatmeal raisin dough can be dropped from a spoon in small mounds. Oat flakes make the mixture look rougher than a smooth cake batter.

supper-at-the-stove-2.solvingTip: Start with the three-letter word for the soup's temperature. Then look for the long-handled tool used between the pot and the bowls.

notes.COVER: Cover is a noun here. It names the lid you lift off the pot before serving, though the same word can name the action of putting it on.
notes.LADLE: A ladle has a deeper bowl and a longer handle than an eating spoon. The handle keeps your hand above the soup as you serve it.

birds-using-familiar-spaces-3.solvingTip: Try the three-letter color clue. Its answer is part of the color name in the clue about the bird.

notes.WORM: An earthworm is one kind of worm. The four squares ask for the shorter word that fits the animal in this yard.
notes.SHOWER: The damp lawn tells you how to read shower here. It was a passing rain outdoors.

clues.DIG: Make a small hole in the soil

watching-at-the-pond-2.solvingTip: Begin with the clue for the rear part of the bird. That can help you with the action that puts it up in the air.

notes.TILT: Only the front of the duck goes under in this scene. Its body is still floating as it leans forward.
notes.SHALLOW: Shallow describes depth. Even a wide pond can be shallow along its edge, where a duck can reach food below the surface.

clues.FEED: Eat, as a duck does at the edge of a pond

pets-at-home.solvingTip: Try the three-letter clue for the animal first. Then look for the clue that describes the deep dish under its nose.

notes.BOWL: Dish can name many kinds of containers. Bowl is more specific, and its deeper sides can also hold the dog's water.

birds-using-familiar-spaces-5.solvingTip: Find the clue for the part that sticks out behind the bird. Then try the one about what it is climbing.

notes.WOODPECKER: A woodpecker can press its stiff tail feathers against a vertical surface for support. That helps it stay in place while its bill taps.
notes.POLE: Pole names an upright support here. The straight piece of wood gives the bird a surface to cling to where you might expect it on a tree.

clues.CLIMB: Go upward, as a bird does on a pole
clues.CLAW: Curved nail a bird uses to grip wood
clues.TAP: Strike lightly, as a beak does against wood

pantry-packets-and-labels-5.solvingTip: Look for the clue for the bowl's bottom first. Then use crossings to work out what the towel does against the counter.

notes.DAMP: A damp towel has some water in it without being soaked. A wrung-out cloth is one example.
notes.GRIP: The towel grips the counter in the sense of resisting a slide. Neither the towel nor the bowl needs a handle for that kind of grip.

clues.COUNTER: Flat kitchen surface where you set a mixing bowl
clues.REST: Sit on a support, as a bowl does on a towel

small-actions-at-the-serving-table.solvingTip: Try the clue for the rounded serving dish. Its letters can help with the word for the part of the spoon a guest can lift.

notes.RIM: Think of where your lips touch a cup. The bowl's rim is the same kind of border, and here it supports the spoon.
notes.REST: Rest is a verb in this clue. Like a book resting on a shelf, the spoon stays up because something underneath supports it.

watching-at-the-pond-4.solvingTip: Start with the three-letter clue for what people breathe. Then try the actions a bubble can take on its way up and at the surface.

notes.BUBBLES: A bubble has air inside it. A ripple is movement along the water and has no pocket of air.
notes.BURST: When a bubble bursts, its thin boundary breaks and the air escapes. The word describes what happens to the bubble itself.

clues.RINGS: Circles that spread outward on the water

watching-at-the-pond-5.solvingTip: Try the short clue for the animal first. Then look for the words that track its movement up and back down.

notes.RINGS: The rings are a shape made by moving water. They start together at the place the fish came up and spread outward.

clues.SPREAD: Move outward, as ripples do on water

breakfast-on-the-griddle-5.solvingTip: Find the short clue for what goes inside the flat bread. Then use its crossings on the clue for bringing one side over.

notes.TORTILLA: The bread needs to bend without cracking to hold the eggs. A crisp tortilla chip is made from similar bread but won't fold that way.
notes.FOLD: A fold brings part of the tortilla over the eggs. A roll would keep turning the tortilla around the filling.

clues.WRAP: Bring the flat bread around the eggs

water-edges-after-weather-4.solvingTip: Start with the clue for the still body of water. Then try the moving water that enters it.

notes.RIPPLES: A ripple travels along the top of the water. The creek can keep flowing into the pond after the small waves have spread out.
notes.CREEK: The important word in the clue is flowing. Even a narrow creek has water moving along a channel, while the pond is mostly still.

animals-around-the-farmyard-2.solvingTip: Begin with the clue for the shallow container. Then try the short action the birds make with their heads at the water.

notes.BILL: A duck's bill is its beak. Here it goes into the water, so this is the animal meaning of the word you might also see on a request for payment.
notes.SPLASH: A duck can dip its bill in very gently. To splash, it moves enough to send some water out of the pan.

clues.FEATHERS: Covering on a bird, including the long ones on its wings
clues.PAN: Shallow metal container that holds water for the ducks

eating-at-the-diner-3.solvingTip: Start with the clue about what rises from the hot cereal. Then use the letters to find the grain named in the dish.

notes.WHEAT: Wheat names the grain that is milled to make the cereal. The finished dish and the grain have separate clues.
notes.CEREAL: Cereal can be served hot or cold. The steam in this diner scene points to a cooked bowl, like oatmeal or hot wheat cereal.

clues.STEAM: What rises visibly from a bowl of very hot cereal
clues.LUMP: Small clump in cereal that should be smooth

neighborhood-pet-care.solvingTip: Try the clue for the wet dirt first. Then look for the cloth you would reach for at the door.

notes.PAWS: A paw print is the mark a paw can leave. The towel dries the dog's feet to keep those marks off the floor.
notes.MUD: Mud has soil in it as well as water. A dog's wet paws can leave a puddle without leaving any dirt.

clues.TOWEL: Absorbent cloth used to dry a dog's wet feet

classic-movie-settings-2.solvingTip: Start with the clue for the water falling from the clouds. Use those letters to find the cover carried above the dancer.

clues.COAT: Outer garment worn over a shirt on a rainy walk
clues.TAP: Light strike a dancer makes with a shoe

notes.SHOE: A tap shoe makes its sound when the metal under it strikes the ground. The toe and heel give the dancer different ways to make a beat.
notes.RAIN: Rain leaves the puddles that are part of the street setting in this musical. The umbrella and coat fit the wet-weather scene.
notes.COAT: The coat is part of the dancer's outfit on the wet street. The umbrella is the piece he opens and moves around while he dances.

old-shop-tools.solvingTip: Try the clue for the person behind the counter. Then picture what a waiting customer does to get that person's attention.

clues.TAP: Give the bell a light strike with a finger

notes.RING: Ring is a verb here. A small tap is the action your finger makes, and ringing is what the bell does in response.

picnic-band-sounds-2.solvingTip: Start with the clue for the small flat pieces around the instrument. Then look for the sound they make when they move.

clues.FRAME: Outer ring that holds the tambourine's metal discs
clues.BEAT: Regular pulse you can count while music plays
clues.HAND: Body part that holds and shakes the instrument
clues.TAP: Strike lightly with your fingers to make a beat

notes.JINGLE: The little metal discs strike one another when the tambourine moves. Several quick touches can make one bright ringing sound.

stairs-and-hallway-3.solvingTip: Start with the soft container for purchases. Then think about the band you lift and the curved support you hang it on.

clues.LOAD: Weight the filled shopping bag puts on the hook
clues.WALL: Upright surface the hook is fastened to

notes.HOOK: The strap hangs over the curve of the hook. The screw is the separate piece that holds the hook to the wall.

everyday-kitchen-repairs-3.solvingTip: Start with the short clue that means droop in the middle. Its crossings can help with the name for the piece underneath the shelf.

clues.BRACKET: Piece fixed under a shelf to hold it up
clues.LOAD: Weight the stack of dishes puts on the shelf
clues.SUPPORT: Hold up the weight of the plates and bowls

notes.SAG: A shelf can be firm at both ends and have its middle bend downward. That bend is what the short clue describes.
notes.SUPPORT: Support is the action of bearing the weight. The bracket is the piece underneath the shelf that does it.

fall-harvest-work-4.solvingTip: Look first for the tool that tells the clerk how heavy the pumpkin is. Then find the word for the units shown on it.

clues.PLATFORM: Flat part of the scale the pumpkin sits on
clues.STAND: Roadside place where shoppers can buy pumpkins
clues.LOAD: Weight resting on the scale's flat surface
clues.STEM: Short plant stalk still attached to the pumpkin

notes.SCALE: The pumpkin rests on the flat platform while the scale shows its weight. The pounds are the units on that reading.

drinks-poured-and-served-2.solvingTip: Try the short clue for what comes out of the cold bin. Then find the tool that holds several pieces as you lift them.

clues.POUR: Tip the scoop so the ice falls into the pitcher
clues.CUBE: Block of ice with six square faces
clues.LOAD: Amount of ice carried in one scoop
clues.FROST: Thin icy coating that can form on a scoop in the freezer

notes.SCOOP: Here the word names the utensil. Its long handle reaches into the bin and its rounded end holds several pieces of ice.

optional-scenes-in-acts-and-joshua-5.solvingTip: Try the clue for the animals in the net. Then look for the plural word for what carried the fishers in Luke's story.

clues.LOAD: Weight of the fish the boats have to carry

notes.CATCH: Catch is a noun here. It means all the fish taken on this trip, which is why the fishers need help from another boat.

water-close-by-5.solvingTip: Look for the clue about the small flat rock first. Then find the two actions that take it across the water and below it.

clues.SINK: Go below the water when the bouncing stops
clues.RING: A circle that widens from the spot where the stone hits

notes.SKIP: The stone travels along the pond in several short bounces. Each touch can leave a circle spreading over the surface.

birds-to-recognize.solvingTip: Start with the hard mouthpart that taps the trunk. Its letters can help you name the outer part of the tree that the bird taps.

clues.CLAW: Curved nail the bird uses to grip the trunk
clues.FEATHER: One stiff part of a woodpecker's tail
clues.INSECT: Six-legged animal a woodpecker may find under bark

notes.BARK: The bird's feet grip the bark, the outer covering of the trunk. The wood lies underneath.
notes.FEATHER: A woodpecker can brace its stiff tail feathers against a trunk. Those feathers help support the bird as its feet grip the bark.
notes.INSECT: Some insects or their young live under bark. A woodpecker can peck at the trunk to reach them with its beak or tongue.

night-outdoors-2.solvingTip: Try the short clue for the bird first. Then look for the word that names the call you might hear from the roof.

clues.HUNT: Look for an animal to catch for food
clues.CLAW: One of the curved nails on an owl's foot
clues.FEATHER: One of the soft-edged parts on an owl's wing

notes.NIGHT: An owl's call can carry through a quiet barnyard after sunset. Dusk is the time when the last daylight fades.
notes.FEATHER: Many owls have soft edges on their flight feathers. Those edges help quiet the sound when the wings move.

kitchen-windowsill-greens-4.solvingTip: Look for the clue about the leaves you can reach first from the edge of the box. Then look for the middle, where the little leaves are growing.

clues.TENDER: Soft and easy to bite, like a young lettuce leaf

notes.OUTER: The outer leaves are the ones farthest from the middle of the plant. Smaller leaves can keep growing in the center.

before-the-first-bite-2.solvingTip: Try the plural clue for the two tools with points. Their letters can help with the action of pulling the chicken into thin pieces.

clues.TENDER: Easy to pull apart, as well-cooked chicken can be

notes.FORKS: One fork holds the chicken still while the other draws away a few strands. Their points do different jobs in the same motion.

welcoming-a-new-neighbor-2.solvingTip: Start with the short message left on the refrigerator. Then look for the word that tells what happens to the trash at the roadside.

clues.PICKUP: Scheduled collection of trash from the curb
clues.CURB: Raised street edge where residents set their trash bins

notes.CURB: The curb marks the edge of the street. That is where the collection truck can reach the bins.

breakfast-on-the-griddle.solvingTip: Start with the word for the browned bread. The longer clue names the narrow pieces cut from it.

clues.PICKUP: Act of lifting a strip of toast from the plate by hand

notes.STRIPS: Cutting from one end of the slice to the other makes longer pieces. Each narrow piece can be lifted separately.

optional-scenes-in-acts-and-joshua.solvingTip: Start with the structure the people walk around. Then use the longer clue for their instruments and the number from the final day in Joshua 6.

clues.SEVEN: How many times the people circle Jericho on the final day in Joshua 6
clues.STEPS: Movements made one at a time while walking
clues.LINE: Row of people walking one behind the next

notes.CIRCLE: The word describes going all the way around the city. Joshua 6 draws a distinction between one circuit on earlier days and seven on the final day.

autumn-kitchen-and-pantry-4.solvingTip: Start with the glass container on the shelf. Then look for the fruit named in the thick topping for toast.

clues.SPREAD: Soft topping you can smooth onto toast
clues.BUTTER: Second word in the name of a thick cooked apple spread
clues.SPOON: Utensil for taking some of the apple mixture from the jar
clues.THICK: Dense enough to stay on a spoon when lifted
clues.FRUIT: Kind of food cooked down to make apple butter
clues.SUGAR: Sweetener found naturally in apples or added to their spread

notes.BUTTER: Apple butter gets its name from its smooth texture. Apples cook down to a thick mixture that spreads easily on toast.
notes.FRUIT: Cooking the fruit slowly lets the apples soften and lets moisture escape. The thick spread gets much of its body from the apples themselves.
notes.SUGAR: Apples bring some sugar of their own to apple butter. As moisture cooks away, their flavor becomes stronger in the thick spread.

lunches-with-a-spoon-4.solvingTip: Try the short clue for the flat bread you dip or spread hummus on. Its letters can help with the longer word for the bean.

clues.SPREAD: Use a spoon to put an even layer of hummus on pita

notes.CHICKPEA: A chickpea is also called a garbanzo bean. Blending the beans gives the bowl of hummus its smooth base.

pantry-choices.solvingTip: Look for the clue for the part you twist off the jar. Then compare the two texture words printed on different peanut butter jars.

clues.BUTTER: Second word on a jar of ground peanuts
clues.SPREAD: Put an even layer of the topping on a slice of toast

kitchen-sandwich-sides-4.solvingTip: Start with the clue for the cooking liquid. Then look for the small dark fruits that get chopped into the topping.

clues.SPREAD: Put a thin layer of the olive topping on bread
clues.PASTE: Thick mixture of chopped olives and oil
clues.CRISP: Firm enough to snap, like the dry toast under the olives

notes.PASTE: Finely chopped olives and oil form a thick mixture that clings to the spoon. The puzzle uses the word for that texture.

kitchen-jars-and-tins.solvingTip: Look for the color of the strips first. Then use the crossings to name the pepper cut into those strips.

clues.SPREAD: Soft cheese mixture that can be smoothed onto a cracker

notes.PIMENTO: Chopped pimentos leave little red pieces in the cheese. They are a mild pepper you may recognize from the center of a stuffed olive.

gift-paper-folds.solvingTip: Try the three-letter clue for the object waved to move air. Then look for the narrow fold that lets it close neatly.

clues.SPREAD: Open the folded paper wide to show its shape

notes.PLEAT: Each pleat is a narrow fold. A row of folds lets the top open out while the base stays together.

keeping-winter-wet-out-2.solvingTip: Find the short clue for what moves around the drying mitten. Then try the clue for the frame that holds it up.

clues.SPREAD: Lay the mitten out so it lies open on the rack
clues.DRIP: A small drop falling from wet clothing

notes.DAMP: A damp mitten still holds a little water. Laying it open lets air reach more of the fabric while that water dries.

watching-small-changes-2.solvingTip: Start with the seasoning that stays on the plate. The other clues explain what the water does before those grains are visible.

clues.SPREAD: Move outward across the plate, as a thin puddle does
clues.TRACE: Very small amount left behind after most of something is gone

notes.GRAINS: As the water evaporates, the dissolved salt stays behind and can form little crystals. Their light color shows up against the plate.

listening-and-looking-outdoors-3.solvingTip: Try the clue for the insect's long supports first. Then look for the little dents those parts make in the water.

clues.SPREAD: Move outward, as a small wave does on the pond

notes.DIMPLES: A dimple is a dip in the surface. A ripple is a small wave that moves across it.

garden-birds-and-insects-3.solvingTip: Start with the short clue for the space between two points. Then look for the word for a single thread crossing that space.

clues.SPREAD: Extend outward as the web gets wider
clues.SILK: Strong fine material a spider makes for its web

notes.ANCHOR: An anchor is a place where a strand is held fast. A leaf or twig can give the spider a fixed point for starting a new thread.

small-habits-of-wild-neighbors-4.solvingTip: Start with the three-letter animal clue. Then find the word for its resting place and the action it takes when it opens its wings.

clues.SPREAD: Open the wings wide as the bat starts to fly
clues.HOLD: Keep the feet in place on the perch
clues.GRIP: Firm grasp the bat releases before it drops

notes.ROOST: A roost is where a bird or bat settles to rest. In this scene the bat lets go of its shelter at dusk.

sauces-and-table-spreads-5.solvingTip: Find the kitchen tool that is warmed first. Then look for the clue that describes the texture of what it will lift.

clues.PORTION: Amount of food set aside for one serving
clues.SPREAD: Soft topping that can be put on bread or crackers

notes.FIRM: The mixture is stiff enough to hold its shape. A spoon can take out one portion while the rest stays in the bowl.

snacks-for-a-table-3.solvingTip: Start with the clue for the round fruit. Then look for the action that moves one cut piece into the peanut butter.

clues.SPREAD: Soft topping such as peanut butter
clues.SLICE: One flat piece cut from the apple
clues.DIP: Put an apple piece briefly into the peanut butter

notes.APPLE: The core holds the seeds. You can cut pieces from around the core and dip the cut edges into the peanut butter.
notes.PLATE: A plate lets you set the apple slices out in a layer instead of a pile. Put the spread beside them so each slice can be dipped.
notes.KNIFE: Cut down beside the apple's core so the seeds stay in the middle piece. The knife can then divide the larger pieces into smaller slices for dipping.

community-volunteers-5.solvingTip: Start with the three-letter clue for what you drink from. Then look for the larger container where the coffee is kept.

clues.HALL: Large room where the church group meets
clues.TAP: Small spout that lets coffee out of the urn
clues.SUGAR: Sweetener set out for guests to stir into coffee

notes.HANDLE: A handle lets you carry or steady the container. The coffee comes out of the little tap at the bottom.
notes.SUGAR: At the coffee table, sugar can be set beside the cups. Each guest can add as much as they like after drawing coffee from the urn.
notes.COFFEE: An urn holds enough coffee for several guests. The small tap lets one person fill a cup at a time while the rest stays in the container.

eating-at-the-diner-2.solvingTip: Try the short clue for the bread first. Then look for what the bees make to sweeten the open halves.

clues.BUTTER: Cream-based topping that melts on warm bread
clues.SPREAD: Smooth an even layer of the topping over a cut half

notes.HONEY: Honey flows slowly. Tiny openings in the soft inside of the roll let a little of it soak in.

garden-small-spaces-2.solvingTip: Try the drink at 10 Across, which you can make with a few mint sprigs. One crossing helps name the green part at 6 Down.

notes.GLASS: The glass is the cup for the finished drink. A mint sprig can rest on top of the ice, where you can smell the leaves as you take a sip.
notes.ROOT: The mint roots anchor the plant near the steps. When you snip a sprig for the glass, the roots stay below the green stems you are cutting.
notes.SCENT: Crushing a mint leaf lightly between your fingers releases its scent. A sprig in the glass brings that same smell close as you sip the tea.

clues.GLASS: Drinking vessel for iced tea with a sprig of mint
clues.SCENT: Fresh smell released by a mint leaf

garden-small-spaces-3.solvingTip: Begin with the short cutting action at 5 Down. Its crossing helps name the bulb at 6 Across whose flavor chives bring to a dish.

clues.STEM: Thin stalk that holds up a chive flower
clues.SCISSORS: Two-bladed tool for snipping chive leaves
clues.ONION: Layered vegetable with a flavor similar to chives

notes.WATER: In a patio pot, the roots take up water from the soil. The narrow green leaves above the soil are the part you cut for a topping.
notes.SCISSORS: Kitchen scissors make it easy to snip a few chive leaves above the soil. You can also use them to cut the long leaves into short pieces for soup.
notes.ONION: Chives and onions are close relatives, which helps explain their similar flavor. In this scene the snipped green leaves give the dish a mild onion taste.

garden-small-spaces-4.solvingTip: Picture what holds the basket up at 8 Down. The crossing at 8 Across asks what you do when you put the basket on that support.

clues.BERRY: Small juicy fruit such as a strawberry
clues.FRUIT: General name for produce such as apples and strawberries
clues.FLOWER: Blossom that comes before a strawberry

notes.WATER: A hanging basket can dry out more quickly than a garden bed. Water goes into the soil in the basket, where the strawberry roots can take it up.
notes.SWEET: Ripe strawberries can taste sweet without any added sugar. Look below the basket's rim as well as over the leaves, since fruit can hang on either side.
notes.FLOWER: The strawberry blossom comes before the ripe berry. After pollination, the middle of the blossom can grow into the red part you eat.

garden-small-spaces-5.solvingTip: Start with what shines on the deck at 2 Down. Then try its crossing at 4 Across, a word for something you could make with the ripe pepper.

notes.SWEET: Sweet describes a kind of pepper with little or no heat. A green sweet pepper often tastes less sugary than the same kind allowed to ripen to red.
notes.GREEN: Many sweet peppers start out green and can change color as they ripen. On some varieties, red is the color they take on later.
notes.SAUCE: A sweet pepper from the deck can become part of a sauce after it is cooked and softened. Blending it turns the softened pieces into a topping you can spoon over food.

clues.SWEET: Mild in flavor, as a pepper without a hot bite
clues.GREEN: Color a sweet pepper often has before it turns red
clues.SAUCE: Pourable topping that can be made from cooked sweet peppers

garden-evening-chores.solvingTip: Find where you stop the water at 1 Across. It shares a square with the twisting action at 1 Down.

clues.REEL: Spool you wind the garden hose around
clues.RUBBER: Flexible material that can let a hose coil onto a reel

notes.REEL: A hose reel holds the tubing in a circle. You can turn it to bring the hose in a little at a time.
notes.WATER: After the tap is turned off, some water can stay in the hose. Lifting one end can help that last bit drain before you wind the hose onto its reel.
notes.RUBBER: Rubber lets a hose bend into a loop when it goes onto the reel. A tight kink can still flatten it enough to block the flow.

garden-evening-chores-3.solvingTip: Try the center of the apple at 10 Down. Its crossing at 9 Across asks for a harvesting action.

notes.SWEET: Ripe fallen apples can vary in sweetness. An apple that tastes sweet by itself can still add a little tartness to a batch of pressed cider.
notes.JUICE: Freshly pressed apple juice can darken as it stands in the air. Color can also vary with the apples that went into the press.
notes.APPLE: An apple that drops from a tree on its own is a windfall. It can have a bruise where it hit the ground even if the peel stays intact.

clues.JUICE: Liquid that comes out when apples are pressed
clues.APPLE: Round fruit that may be gathered after it drops from a tree

garden-evening-chores-4.solvingTip: Start with what you write on an envelope to remember when you saved the seeds at 6 Across. The crossing at 5 Down names what the envelope is made of.

notes.PAPER: A paper envelope can hold seeds once they are dry. Write the plant name and date on the outside so you can tell it from other saved seed.
notes.SEED: The dry seed is what can grow next season. Let the marigold heads dry so the seeds come out more easily before you fill and label the envelope.
notes.ENVELOPE: A closed paper envelope keeps the tiny seeds together. Fold the flap down firmly so the seeds stay inside when the envelope is moved.

clues.PAPER: Material used to make envelopes for saved seeds
clues.ENVELOPE: Folded paper holder you can use to store dried seeds

garden-evening-chores-5.solvingTip: Picture the patch of soil that gets a layer of mulch at 3 Down. It crosses the little unwanted plant at 4 Across.

clues.LOAD: Amount of mulch the wheelbarrow is carrying
clues.HANDLE: One of the two grips used to push a wheelbarrow
clues.WHEEL: Round part at the front of a wheelbarrow that rolls on the path

notes.HANDLE: A wheelbarrow usually has two long handles, one for each hand. Lifting them shifts the load onto the front wheel so it can roll.
notes.WHEEL: One front wheel carries much of the load in a typical wheelbarrow. As it rolls, the two handles let you guide the wheel along the path and steady the load.

garden-from-the-beginning.solvingTip: Look at 1 Across for a line of seedlings. Its crossing at 1 Down names the part growing down into the soil.

clues.MIST: Spray a light cloud of water over the seedlings
clues.NAME: Word on a marker that tells which plant is growing
clues.LIGHT: Brightness that helps seedlings grow above the soil
clues.PENCIL: Writing tool for marking a wooden plant tag

notes.LABEL: The label is the marker itself. The word on it tells you which plant is growing in that spot.
notes.LIGHT: Light reaches the seedlings above the soil. The markers can face the front of the tray so you can read the names without moving the young plants.
notes.PENCIL: A pencil can leave a readable mark on some plant tags made of unfinished wood. Write the name and date before pushing the tag into the tray.

garden-from-the-beginning-2.solvingTip: Find the glass container at 7 Down. Then try the crossing at 9 Across for how the paper feels when it is a little wet.

clues.WATCH: Look closely as the first root appears
clues.GLASS: Clear material that lets you watch a seed grow in a jar
clues.PAPER: Sheet material kept damp beside a bean as it sprouts

notes.WATCH: Watch is an action here. The clear jar lets you see the little root grow without moving the bean.
notes.GLASS: The glass wall lets you watch a root develop without digging up the bean. A damp paper lining can hold the seed where you can see it.
notes.PAPER: Damp paper holds the bean against the side of the jar without covering it with soil. That leaves the root visible as it starts to grow.

garden-from-the-beginning-4.solvingTip: Try the long-handled garden tool at 1 Down. It crosses the straight mark or guide at 2 Across.

clues.LINE: Straight mark or guide for spacing the onions
clues.SKIN: Thin papery covering on the outside of an onion
clues.BULB: Round part of an onion made of layers
clues.ONION: Layered vegetable grown from sets in a garden row

notes.WHITE: White and red describe common kinds of onion. The dry outer layer of a white onion is pale, and the fleshy layers inside can look almost clear when sliced thin.
notes.ONION: Small onion bulbs planted in spring are often called sets. Each can grow into a larger onion if there is room between the plants in the row.
notes.ROOT: The onion's small roots spread from its flat bottom into the soil. The layered bulb grows above that cluster of roots.

garden-from-the-beginning-5.solvingTip: Begin with the tool at 6 Down that cuts the young squash from its stem. Use a crossing for the longer squash name at 8 Across.

clues.SKIN: Outside covering of the young squash
clues.STEM: Stalk that holds the squash on the plant
clues.SUMMER: Warm season when young zucchini is often picked
clues.KNIFE: Bladed tool for cutting a young squash from the vine

notes.BASKET: A young zucchini has tender skin that can bruise. A shallow basket lets you carry the squash without piling heavier produce on top.
notes.SUMMER: Zucchini is often picked in summer before the squash reaches its full size. At that stage the skin is tender enough to leave on for cooking.
notes.KNIFE: A garden knife can cut through the firm stem above a young zucchini. That lets the squash come free without pulling the vine along with it.

garden-welcoming-corners.solvingTip: Find the edge of the shallow bowl at 3 Down. It shares a square with the bird with the orange-red breast at 3 Across.

notes.WATER: A shallow layer of water gives a small bird a place to stand while it splashes. The raised rim is another place for birds to perch.
notes.FEATHER: After splashing in a birdbath, a bird may shake water from its feathers. It can use its beak to arrange them again as they dry.

garden-welcoming-corners-2.solvingTip: Begin with the long seat at 9 Across. Then try the crossing for the part of the shrub that hangs above it at 5 Down.

notes.BRANCH: Lilac flower clusters grow near the ends of woody stems. A branch reaches out over the bench, holding the blooms above the seat.
notes.BLOOM: A cluster on a lilac can hold many small blooms. The open blossoms release the scent you can notice when you sit beneath them.
notes.BENCH: The bench gives two people a place to sit beneath the lilac. Narrow gaps between wooden slats can let rainwater run off the seat.

clues.BRANCH: Woody part of a lilac that reaches out above a bench
clues.BLOOM: One open flower in a lilac cluster

garden-welcoming-corners-3.solvingTip: Start with the bright object that makes a shadow at 9 Across. A crossing leads to what holds the sundial up at 7 Down.

notes.LIGHT: Sunlight striking the raised part of the sundial casts a shadow across the face. As the shadow moves, it points to different hour marks.
notes.GARDEN: A sundial can stand in an open part of a garden. A nearby wall or tall plant can shade it and hide the moving shadow, so an open spot gives you more hours to read it.
notes.NUMBER: A number on a sundial marks an hour. Follow the shadow to the numbered line, or look between two lines for an approximate time.

clues.LIGHT: What the sun provides so a sundial can cast a shadow
clues.GARDEN: Outdoor growing area where you might set a sundial
clues.NUMBER: Mark on a sundial that identifies one of its hours

garden-welcoming-corners-4.solvingTip: Look at 7 Down for the time when daylight begins to fade. The crossing at 11 Across asks what softens the lantern's glare.

clues.SHADE: Cover around the lantern's light that softens its glare
clues.HANDLE: Loop you hold to carry a lantern

notes.SHADE: A lantern shade can shield your eyes from the brightest part and send more light toward the path.
notes.HANDLE: The loop at the top of a lantern can serve two jobs. You can carry the lantern by it or slip it over a hook.
notes.LIGHT: A hanging lantern casts light down onto the path. At dusk, the glow can help show where the edge of the walk is.

garden-welcoming-corners-5.solvingTip: Try the footwear that keeps mud off your foot at 5 Across. Its crossing names the walking route through the beds at 2 Down.

clues.STONE: Hard piece of rock set into the garden path
clues.MUD: Wet soil a boot can pick up beside the stones
clues.BOOT: Footwear that covers the ankle when walking between garden beds

notes.STONE: Set underfoot, a broad stone gives you a firm spot to step. It keeps your boot above the softer soil beside it.
notes.BOOT: A garden boot can gather mud in the grooves of its sole. Short steps between the flat stones help keep it from sinking into loose ground.

garden-keeping-tools.solvingTip: Picture the curved support on the shed wall at 2 Across. The crossing at 2 Down asks for the part of a tool you hold.

clues.FORK: Garden tool with points for loosening soil

notes.FORK: The long points of a garden fork loosen packed earth. Pressing down on the top helps those points go into the soil.
notes.HANDLE: A trowel has a short handle so you can work close to the soil. Some handles have a hole at the end, which lets the tool hang on a hook.

garden-keeping-tools-2.solvingTip: Begin with the part of the fence that swings open at 7 Down. It crosses the action you take to shut it at 11 Across.

notes.HANDLE: The handle gives you a grip for pulling the gate shut. The latch is the separate part that catches and holds the gate there.
notes.PAINT: A fresh coat of paint can cover exposed wood after a gate is repaired. The hinge still needs room to move as the paint dries.
notes.FENCE: The fence stays in place as the gate swings on its hinges. If the gate sags, the post may need to be checked as well as the hinge.

clues.HANDLE: Part you pull to close a garden gate
clues.PAINT: Liquid coating that can cover bare wood on a repaired gate

garden-keeping-tools-3.solvingTip: Start with the part that covers the barrel at 7 Down. Then use a crossing to find what water does when it runs out at 9 Across.

notes.RAIN: Rain that lands on the roof can run into a gutter and down a spout. A barrel set below the spout can collect part of that water.
notes.SCREEN: A screen at the top of a rain barrel can let runoff through and catch leaves from the gutter. The collected water stays below that mesh.
notes.BARREL: A barrel below a downspout stores runoff for later use. Put the tap low on the side so you can fill a watering can without reaching into the barrel.

clues.RAIN: Water from clouds that can collect in a barrel
clues.SCREEN: Mesh that lets water into a barrel while catching leaves
clues.BARREL: Large container that collects water from a downspout

garden-keeping-tools-4.solvingTip: Try the inside surface of your hand at 10 Across. The crossing at 6 Down is what you do when you hold a tool securely.

notes.COTTON: Cotton can be woven into the back or cuff of a garden glove. Some pairs use a tougher material on the palm, which does most of the gripping.
notes.HAND: The glove protects the parts of the hand that do most of the work, including the fingers and palm. The cuff sits above them at the wrist.

clues.COTTON: Plant fiber sometimes used for a garden glove's back or cuff
clues.HAND: Body part protected by a gardening glove

garden-keeping-tools-5.solvingTip: Find the short action at 3 Down for what the shears do. Its crossing at 4 Across names one woody plant in the hedge.

clues.LEVEL: Flat and even in height along the top
clues.TRIM: Make the whole hedge neat by cutting along its top
clues.CLIP: Snip off a single leaf or twig with one quick motion
clues.BRANCH: Woody part of a hedge that can be trimmed back

notes.LEVEL: Level describes the result along the top. You can compare the height at both ends to see whether one side is higher.
notes.BRANCH: A branch has older woody growth under its leaves. Shears trim the smaller tips to even out the hedge, while a bigger branch may need a different tool.
notes.GREEN: The hedge looks green where the leafy shoots cover its branches. A deep cut into old wood can expose bare areas under that outer layer.

garden-fruit-trees.solvingTip: Look first for the fruit at 6 Down that is wider at the bottom. It shares a square with the seed-bearing center at 9 Across.

clues.STEM: Short stalk attaching the pear to the branch
clues.YELLOW: Ripe-lemon color that can appear on pear skin

notes.YELLOW: Some pear varieties change from green to yellow as they ripen. The skin color is only one sign, since other varieties can stay green when ripe.
notes.BASKET: Set the pears in the basket gently as you pick them. A shallow layer helps keep the fruit underneath from being pressed by the rest.
notes.BRANCH: A pear hangs from a short fruit stem attached to the branch or a smaller offshoot. The stem can come away with the fruit while the branch stays on the tree.

garden-fruit-trees-2.solvingTip: Find the hard piece in the middle of a peach at 7 Across. The crossing at 6 Down describes when the fruit is ready to pick.

notes.SLICE: Peach slices can be cut away from the pit one at a time. A soft ripe peach is easier to slice without pressing hard on the skin.
notes.FRUIT: The peach is a fruit with a single hard pit. Fuzzy skin and soft flesh can help you recognize it before the pit is visible.
notes.PEACH: Ripe peaches can bruise when they are pressed against one another. Set them gently into the basket so the softer fruit at the bottom stays whole.

clues.FRUIT: Food group that includes peaches and plums
clues.PEACH: Fuzzy fruit you can pick and carry in a basket

garden-fruit-trees-3.solvingTip: Start with the dish that holds the washed plums at 5 Across. Follow its crossing at 2 Down to the flavor that reminds you of sugar.

clues.PICK: Gather ripe plums from the branches
clues.PIT: Hard center stone removed from a plum

notes.PICK: Pick names the action of taking a plum off its branch. The fruit still has its hard center when you carry it inside.
notes.SWEET: A ripe plum can have sweet flesh next to a rather tart skin. You may notice both tastes in the same bite.
notes.FRUIT: A plum is a stone fruit, so its juicy flesh surrounds one hard pit. That is also why a plum can be cut into pieces that lift away from the center.

garden-fruit-trees-4.solvingTip: Think of a baked dessert with a cherry filling at 10 Across. At 10 Down, the crossing asks for the hard center you take out before baking.

clues.STEM: Thin stalk that attaches a cherry to the branch
clues.JUICE: Liquid released when a cherry is cut or crushed

notes.BASKET: Use a small basket for cherries so the top layer stays within reach. Some cherries may come off the branch with their paired stems still joined.
notes.JUICE: A ripe cherry can release red juice when you cut it or remove its pit. The liquid is what can leave a colored spot on the cutting board.
notes.CHERRY: Cherries on the same tree can ripen at slightly different times. The deeper color of one cherry can be a sign to pick it, while a paler one may need more time.

garden-fruit-trees-5.solvingTip: Try the sharp taste at 10 Across. Use one of its letters to help with the yellow citrus fruit at 5 Down.

clues.JUICE: Liquid squeezed from the flesh of a lemon
clues.WHEEL: Rolling part under a plant tub that helps it move

notes.JUICE: Squeezing the lemon releases liquid from its flesh. The rind is the outside layer and can be used separately.
notes.WHEEL: A wheel under the tub can take part of the weight of the soil. With the tub on a wheeled stand, you can move the tree toward a sunnier spot.
notes.LEMON: A lemon on a small tree grows from a flower. Moving the tub makes it possible to give the plant more sun as the fruit develops.

animals-on-the-farm.solvingTip: Start with the adult bird leading the young chicks at 2 Down. The crossing at 5 Across asks what a chick hatches from.

notes.FEATHER: A chick's first covering is usually soft down. As it grows, longer feathers appear, including the ones along the wings.
notes.BEAK: The hen scratches with her feet and uses her beak to pick up what she uncovers. Her chicks can peck at small bits on the ground as they follow her.

animals-on-the-farm-3.solvingTip: Find what covers the lamb and can be spun into yarn at 7 Down. It crosses the color clue at 7 Across.

notes.GRASS: Grass is what the ewes can graze on while the lamb rests nearby. The pasture is the whole area where the flock feeds and stays together.
notes.SPRING: New grass starts to come up as the pasture warms in spring. The flock can move across the open ground to feed on that fresh growth.
notes.SHEEP: A lamb is a young sheep. It can stay near its mother in the pasture even while she moves around to graze.

clues.GRASS: Narrow-leaved plants that sheep can graze on
clues.SPRING: Season when fresh grass often returns to a pasture

animals-on-the-farm-4.solvingTip: Look for the short name for a young goat at 9 Down. Use a crossing for the hair on the adult goat's chin at 10 Across.

notes.FENCE: A goat may raise its front feet onto a sturdy part of the fence to see over it. If the fence has horizontal rails, spaces between them also give it a view through to the hay.
notes.TAIL: A goat usually carries its short tail raised. The long hair under its chin is the beard, a feature you can see from across the fence.
notes.GATE: A gate is the part that can swing to make a gap in the goat's enclosure. A latch holds it in line with the posts when the gap is closed.

clues.FENCE: Barrier with posts that a goat might look over
clues.GATE: Movable part of an enclosure that can open and close

animals-on-the-farm-5.solvingTip: Try the body part used for hearing at 5 Across. Its crossing helps with the name at 2 Down for an animal with a donkey father and a horse mother.

notes.TAIL: A donkey can flick its tail at flies near its hind legs. The tail often has a tuft of longer hair at the end.
notes.CART: A cart is a wheeled carrier a working donkey can pull. The wheels support the load as the animal draws it forward.

clues.TAIL: Part at a donkey's rear that often ends in a tuft of hair

small-wild-visitors.solvingTip: Begin with how a rabbit moves in one short jump at 9 Down. Then look at the crossing for the part it uses to sniff at 10 Across.

notes.GRASS: A rabbit can feed on grass near a blackberry bush and move under the branches for cover. The bush and the low growth underneath give it different places to hide.
notes.SOFT: Soft describes how the rabbit's fur feels. The fur lies close against its body as it ducks under the low blackberry branches.
notes.PAW: A rabbit pushes off with its larger back paws when it hops. Its smaller front paws touch down as it comes to a stop under the bush.

clues.GRASS: Low green growth a rabbit may eat beside a bush
clues.SOFT: Gentle and pleasant to the touch, like a rabbit's fur
clues.PAW: Clawed foot a rabbit lands on

small-wild-visitors-2.solvingTip: Start with the hard-shelled food a chipmunk might carry at 4 Across. The crossing at 5 Down names the part behind its body.

clues.PAW: Foot a chipmunk uses to hold a seed
clues.SEED: Small plant part a chipmunk may carry in its cheek pouch

notes.SEED: A chipmunk can tuck several seeds into its cheek pouches. The pouches help it carry the seeds away from the step in one trip.
notes.TAIL: A chipmunk can hold its tail out behind it while crossing the stone step. The stripes that help identify it are mainly along its back.
notes.PAW: A chipmunk can grip a seed between its front paws while it nibbles. Those same paws can steady it when it scampers across the step.

small-wild-visitors-3.solvingTip: Try the covering that the raccoon's dark eye markings resemble at 10 Across. Its crossing at 6 Down names the small stream beside it.

clues.MASK: Face covering the raccoon's dark eye markings resemble
