clues.HANDLE: Part of a gas nozzle you hold while filling the tank
clues.PRICE: Amount shown per gallon at a gas pump
clues.RECEIPT: Record of payment for fuel at a gas pump

notes.HANDLE: The handle is the part of the pump nozzle you hold. The lever under your fingers controls when the fuel flows.
notes.PRICE: The pump shows a price per gallon. Its running total rises as more fuel goes into the tank, and the receipt can show both figures.
notes.RECEIPT: A receipt from a gas pump can identify the station, date, and time. That can help you recognize the purchase later if you paid for more than one fill-up on a trip.

on-the-local-road-4.solvingTip: Find what you turn to start the engine at 9 Across. Then try its crossing for what the dashboard tells you about how fast you are going at 8 Down.

clues.KEY: Metal piece turned to start many older cars
clues.WHEEL: Round control a driver turns to steer
clues.MIRROR: Reflective surface a driver uses to see behind the car

notes.WHEEL: The wheel here is the large ring the driver turns by hand. The dashboard sits behind it so you can see the gauges through or above the ring.
notes.MIRROR: The inside rearview mirror shows part of the road behind the car. You can see it by glancing up from the dashboard.

on-the-local-road-5.solvingTip: Try the sleeveless garment that helps drivers see the crossing guard at 4 Across. Its crossing names where the children are headed at 5 Down.

clues.VEST: Bright sleeveless garment worn by a crossing guard
clues.SCHOOL: Place children cross the street to get to for class
clues.FLAG: Small cloth signal a crossing guard may hold up

notes.SCHOOL: A school can be close to a busy road. A crossing guard helps children get from the curb to the other side on the way to or from class.
notes.FLAG: A flag can be a small signal a person raises so others see it. At the crossing, the guard uses a visible signal to get attention before the children walk.

community-volunteers.solvingTip: Begin with the carton on the donation table at 4 Across. A crossing leads to the general word for what you put in it at 1 Down.

notes.SHELF: At the pantry, a shelf can hold one group of donations, such as soup cans or bags of rice. Grouping similar foods helps people see what is available.
notes.LABEL: A label on a donated can or box helps you sort it without opening it. A shelf label can then show visitors where to find the same kind of food.
notes.RICE: A sealed bag of dry rice can sit with other shelf-stable donations. Keeping the label facing outward lets someone see the type of rice without opening the bag.

clues.SHELF: Flat storage surface at the pantry for donations
clues.RICE: Grain often donated in bags to a food pantry

community-volunteers-2.solvingTip: Try the action that bends the program in half at 1 Across. It crosses the detail printed to tell people when the concert is held at 2 Down.

clues.COVER: Outside sheet of a printed concert program
clues.PRINT: Put the concert program's words on paper

notes.PAPER: The printed sheet becomes a program when it is folded so the pages read in order. The title and date can go on the outside.
notes.PRINT: Print a test copy before making a stack of concert programs. Folding that first sheet shows whether the cover and song list land on the right sides.

community-volunteers-3.solvingTip: Look at 5 Down for the line made by chairs set next to one another. It crosses the part of the room visitors open when they arrive at 4 Across.

clues.FOLD: Bring the seat and legs of a chair together for storage
clues.TABLE: Flat surface at the front of a meeting for papers or supplies
clues.CHAIR: Seat for one person that may fold after a meeting
clues.CIRCLE: Round shape made by chairs facing one another

notes.TABLE: A table at the front can hold meeting notes or a sign-in sheet. The chairs can face it while leaving an aisle open.
notes.CHAIR: A folding chair can be opened as people arrive and stored again after the meeting. Leave a gap between rows so people can reach their places.
notes.CIRCLE: When seats form a circle, the people sitting in them can face one another. A gap between two chairs gives people a way into the middle.

community-volunteers-4.solvingTip: Start with the little label showing what the book costs at 2 Down. Use the crossing for one numbered side of the paper inside at 5 Across.

notes.TABLE: Make a few stacks on the table so shoppers can see the subjects or authors. A box under the table can hold extra books until there is room to display them.
notes.PRICE: At a book sale, a price tag can go on each book, or a sign can cover a whole group such as paperbacks. Putting like books together makes the sign easier to use.
notes.PAGE: Before pricing a used book, fan its pages and look for tears or loose paper. The cover alone may hide wear inside.

clues.TABLE: Raised surface where used books can be displayed for sale
clues.PAGE: One side of a leaf in a used book

keeping-in-touch.solvingTip: Find the word for contacting a friend by telephone at 12 Across. Its crossing leads to what you do with the digits before they pick up at 10 Down.

clues.LINE: Phone connection you and your friend speak over
clues.DIAL: Enter the digits to place a phone call
clues.LISTEN: Pay attention to what a friend says on the phone

notes.NUMBER: The phone number tells the telephone system which person or line you want to reach. You can tap the digits or use a saved contact.
notes.VOICE: The voice you hear over the phone can be familiar before your friend says a name. The way a person speaks can come through even though you cannot see them.
notes.LISTEN: On a phone call, listening means leaving room for your friend to finish a thought. A short pause can make it easier to hear what they say next.

keeping-in-touch-2.solvingTip: Try the tool for writing the message on the card at 8 Down. A crossing helps name what you do when you put the card in the mail at 10 Across.

notes.STAMP: A postcard has room for its stamp on the address side. The picture fills the other side and stays visible during the trip home.
notes.ADDRESS: A postcard usually has a space for the address on the right below the stamp. The short greeting can fit on the other side of the writing area.
notes.HOME: Send home means mail the postcard back to the place you came from. The picture on the card can show someone there what you saw on the trip.

clues.STAMP: Small postage label that goes on a postcard
clues.ADDRESS: Details written on a postcard to tell where it should go

keeping-in-touch-3.solvingTip: Start with the greeting you make with your hand at 7 Down. It shares a square with the word for the moving picture that lets family see you at 9 Across.

clues.SCREEN: Flat display where you see the family during the call
clues.FAMILY: Relatives you might greet on a video call
clues.CAMERA: Device that shows your face to family on a video call

notes.SCREEN: The screen shows the other person. The camera on your device sends your picture back to them.
notes.FAMILY: A family call can link relatives in different places. If several people sit near one screen, moving back a little can help everyone fit in the camera's view.
notes.CAMERA: On many devices the camera is near the top of the screen. Looking toward it as you wave can make the greeting feel more direct to the people on the call.

keeping-in-touch-4.solvingTip: Try the word that tells how old the person is at 11 Across. Its crossing names the time that has passed between two birthdays at 10 Down.

notes.STAMP: The stamp is usually near the top corner of the birthday card's envelope. The greeting with the person's name is inside the envelope.
notes.NAME: The name on the envelope tells who is meant to receive the birthday card. The greeting inside can use a familiar nickname the person will recognize.
notes.CANDLE: A birthday candle stands in the icing so it can be lit for the wish. On a birthday card, a drawing of one can suggest the celebration even without a picture of the whole party.

clues.CANDLE: Small wax light set in birthday cake icing

keeping-in-touch-5.solvingTip: Find the short written message at 8 Across. Its crossing points to what holds it against the refrigerator at 5 Down.

clues.HOLD: Keep the paper from sliding down the refrigerator door
clues.DOOR: Movable refrigerator panel you can put a reminder on

notes.DOOR: The reminder sits on the outside of the refrigerator door, where you can see it as you go by. A magnet lets you take it down or move it when the plan changes.
notes.PHONE: A note may include a phone number you need later. Keeping it on the refrigerator lets you read the digits before you place the call.

shopping-basket.solvingTip: Look at 9 Down for what you push down the aisle. Then use a crossing to name the written reminder of what goes into it at 12 Across.

notes.BASKET: The basket is the part of a grocery cart that holds the groceries. On many carts it is made of metal wire, and the wheels are on the frame below.
notes.HANDLE: Push the cart using the bar across the back. That handle is outside the basket, so your hands can stay clear of the groceries.

clues.BASKET: Part of a grocery cart that holds the items
clues.HANDLE: Bar at the back that you hold to push a shopping cart

shopping-basket-2.solvingTip: Try the unit represented by one penny at 8 Down. It shares a square with the amount printed on the shelf label at 7 Across.

notes.SHELF: At some stores, the shelf label shows a price for the whole package and one for a standard amount, such as an ounce. The second number can help compare packages of different sizes.
notes.PRICE: A sale tag may show a lower price for one size or variety. Check the name and size on the tag to match it to the right package.
notes.LABEL: The package label gives details such as the product name and net weight. Matching those details to the tag on the shelf helps you read the price for the right package.

clues.SHELF: Flat surface where store packages sit above price tags
clues.LABEL: Printed information panel that can show a package's weight

shopping-basket-3.solvingTip: Find the handled bag you bring from home at 11 Across. Its crossing names what you do when you bring it back for another shopping trip at 7 Down.

notes.HANDLE: A reusable bag may have two cloth handles sewn into its seams. The stitching spreads the pull from the weight of the groceries.
notes.STITCH: One stitch can be made by passing the needle in and out of the cloth. A row of these small stitches joins the cloth edges into a seam.
notes.GROCERY: Grocery describes what the bag is used to carry home from the store. A wide bottom helps boxes sit flat on the way home.

clues.HANDLE: Loop you hold when lifting a cloth shopping bag
clues.GROCERY: ___ bag, a sack for carrying purchases home from the food store

shopping-basket-4.solvingTip: Look for the coin worth ten cents at 9 Down. Its crossing helps with the unit worth four quarters at 9 Across.

clues.BILL: Piece of paper money used to pay at the checkout
clues.RECEIPT: Checkout record that can show your change due
clues.CHANGE: Money the cashier returns when you pay more than the total

notes.RECEIPT: The checkout receipt can show the total, the cash received, and the change due. If you count your change, that last line gives you a figure to compare it with.
notes.CHANGE: On a bill of seventy-five cents paid with a dollar, the change is twenty-five cents. The cashier might hand back a quarter or several smaller coins.

shopping-basket-5.solvingTip: Try the metal container you set beside the jars at 8 Across. Then look at its crossing for what you do when you take the groceries out at 7 Down.

notes.FRUIT: When unpacking fruit, look for ripe or bruised pieces that can be used sooner. Firmer pieces can wait until later.
notes.COUNTER: A kitchen counter gives you room to see what came out of each bag. Bottles can stand at the back while boxes and small cans are sorted in front.
notes.GROCERY: Groceries are the items brought home from the food store. Putting milk and other chilled items away first clears space to sort the boxes and cans.

clues.FRUIT: Produce such as apples, pears, or oranges
clues.COUNTER: Kitchen surface where you can set out groceries
clues.GROCERY: Word before shopping for the trip to buy household food

small-town-outings.solvingTip: Begin with what you do with your hands after a performance at 3 Across. It crosses the person playing a character onstage at 2 Down.

clues.ACTOR: Person who plays a character onstage
clues.USHER: Person who helps visitors find their theater seats
clues.TICKET: Pass that gets you into a show

notes.USHER: The usher can read the row and seat number on a ticket. The seat itself may have a small number plate.
notes.LIGHT: The theater can lower the light in the seating area as the show is about to start. Light on the stage helps the audience see the actors once the curtain opens.
notes.TICKET: At the theater door, a ticket shows that the holder can go in. It may also carry the performance time so the holder knows which show it is for.

small-town-outings-3.solvingTip: Find what you read before telling the server what you want at 6 Down. Its crossing names the corner place that serves the meal at 8 Across.

notes.TABLE: The cafe table is where you read the menu, eat, and receive the bill. The counter is a different place where some customers might order to go.
notes.WINDOW: A table by a cafe window gives diners a view of the corner while they wait for their order. Daylight through the glass can also make the menu easier to read.
notes.CHAIR: Pull the chair out far enough to sit before settling in to read the menu. At a small cafe, the space between tables can also be the waiter's route.

clues.WINDOW: Glass opening that lets cafe diners see the street

small-town-outings-4.solvingTip: Look for the part you open to enter the garden at 8 Down. The crossing names the barrier it is attached to at 10 Across.

notes.WATER: A shared water supply is useful even when everyone grows a different crop. Look for where each gardener can fill a watering can or attach a hose.
notes.FENCE: A fence can mark the outside of the garden, while paths and plot signs show the smaller spaces within it. A gate gives gardeners a place to enter with their tools.
notes.GARDEN: The community garden may have several plots tended by different people. A plot sign can tell you who grows food or flowers in one part of the shared space.

clues.FENCE: Barrier that can mark the outside of a community garden
clues.GARDEN: Shared growing area where neighbors may tend separate plots

small-town-outings-5.solvingTip: Find the price of the ride at 3 Down. Its crossing leads to the covered place that keeps rain off people waiting at 6 Across.

notes.BENCH: The shelter bench gives you a place to sit while waiting near the stop sign. If the road is visible from there, you can watch for your bus as it approaches.
notes.ROUTE: A route is the course a bus follows from stop to stop. Checking the route number on the shelter sign helps you find the bus that goes where you want.
notes.SHELTER: A bus shelter can have a roof and side panels. The roof keeps rain off the bench, and a side panel can block some wind while you wait.

clues.BENCH: Long seat for people waiting under a bus shelter
clues.SHELTER: Covered place to wait for the bus

home-storage-spaces.solvingTip: Try the action of bringing one edge of a towel over the other at 7 Down. Its crossing names the level surface where you put it away at 6 Across.

clues.CASE: Cloth covering that slips over a pillow

notes.SHELF: The closet shelf can hold matching sheets and pillowcases in one pile. A separate pile of towels is easy to spot when you open the door.
notes.COTTON: Cotton sheets and towels can sit in separate stacks in the linen closet. Linen in the name of the closet refers to household cloth items, whatever fiber they use.
notes.SHEET: Fold a loose sheet down to the width of the shelf before putting it away. A fitted sheet folds more neatly if you tuck its elastic corners into one another first.

home-storage-spaces-2.solvingTip: Look for the utensil with prongs at 3 Down. It crosses the compartment you pull open to put that utensil away at 5 Across.

notes.HANDLE: In the utensil drawer, lining up the handles toward the front gives your hand an easy place to grab. The other ends are the parts used for cutting, stirring, or lifting food.
notes.DRAWER: A drawer can have short compartments for eating utensils and a longer one for cooking tools. The different lengths leave room for the handles of a whisk or ladle.
notes.KNIFE: Kitchen knives can go in a long compartment of the utensil drawer. Keeping them in their own space makes the blade end easier to see when you reach for another tool.

home-storage-spaces-3.solvingTip: Try the little cubes you roll to get a number at 2 Across. Use one crossing for the flat piece you might draw from a deck at 3 Down.

notes.SHELF: A wide shelf can keep game boxes level with their lids closed. Small pieces stay with the right board when each box goes back together.
notes.PIECE: A game piece can stand for one player and show how far that player has moved. Its color or shape helps keep it distinct from the others.

clues.SHELF: Flat surface that holds boxes of board games
clues.PIECE: One small item you move around a game board

home-storage-spaces-4.solvingTip: Start with the cord you tie across the top of a shoe at 8 Across. Its crossing names the open stand where the pair goes at 7 Down.

notes.BRUSH: A shoe brush can sit on the rack beside the footwear. Soft bristles can wipe away loose dust before the shoes are put on again.
notes.DOOR: The back door is where wet or dusty shoes can come off after you step inside. A rack beside the door gives the pairs a place to wait off the floor.
notes.LACE: Tuck the loose ends of each lace inside its shoe before setting the pair on the rack. That keeps the strings out of the doorway.

clues.BRUSH: Bristled tool you might leave by a shoe rack
clues.LACE: String you might tuck into a shoe on the rack

home-storage-spaces-5.solvingTip: Find the lidded container for the clothes at 9 Across. Then look at its crossing for the word for a part of the year, like summer, at 6 Down.

notes.SUMMER: When summer ends, shorts and sandals can be put away together. A label lets you identify the warm-weather clothes without opening every box.
notes.LABEL: A storage label can name both the season and the kind of clothes inside. Those few words can tell a box of shorts from a box of sandals.
notes.SHIRT: A lightweight summer shirt can go in the same labeled box as the shorts. Folding the sleeves inward keeps them from sticking out when you stack the shirts.

clues.LABEL: Tag that tells what clothes are in a storage box

the-family-car.solvingTip: Look for what you apply to the clean car to give it a shine at 9 Across. Its crossing names what made the suds earlier at 8 Down.

clues.WAX: Coating rubbed on clean car paint to make it shine
clues.WINDOW: Glass panel at the side of a car

notes.WATER: Clean water from a hose can rinse loose grit off the car before a sponge touches the paint. Rinsing again takes away the suds.
notes.WINDOW: The car window is the glass beside a seat. Rinsing the edge first can carry away grit that would otherwise get dragged across the glass.

the-family-car-2.solvingTip: Try the folded sheet showing where towns are at 9 Across. Its crossing names what you drive along to reach one of them at 7 Down.

notes.FOLD: A paper road map opens along its folds. Unfold the panels around your route so you can follow a highway from one town to the next.
notes.ROUTE: A driving route connects the roads and turns that get you to your destination. You can pick out a place to stop along the way before you leave.

clues.FOLD: Bend a map back along a crease

the-family-car-3.solvingTip: Find the vehicle with the trunk you are loading at 2 Down. Then use a crossing for the word for a journey away from home at 5 Across.

clues.LATCH: Fastening that keeps the car's trunk shut
clues.HANDLE: Part of a suitcase you hold to lift it into the trunk
clues.BLANKET: Soft covering you could pack in the car for a picnic
clues.BAG: Soft carrying case that can fit beside a suitcase

notes.HANDLE: The suitcase handle is for lifting the case into the trunk. After the bags are inside, the latch holds the trunk lid shut.
notes.BLANKET: A folded blanket can travel in the car trunk and be spread out at a stop. Its soft layers can also sit between packed items to keep them from rubbing.
notes.BAG: A soft bag can fit beside a suitcase in the trunk. Put it near the opening if it holds something you expect to use at the first stop.

the-family-car-4.solvingTip: Try the part that swings back and forth and holds the blade at 5 Down. Its crossing asks how the windshield looks when you see through it easily at 4 Across.

clues.ARM: Part that swings the windshield wiper blade back and forth
clues.WATER: Clear liquid a wiper sweeps from the windshield
clues.RAIN: Water from clouds that a wiper clears from the windshield
clues.SWEEP: Move across the windshield to clear away water

notes.RUBBER: The flexible rubber strip rests against the glass and sweeps rain away. The rigid arm moves the whole blade back and forth.
notes.WATER: Drops of rain left on the windshield can blur the view. The rubber edge of a wiper pushes that water aside as the wiper arm swings.
notes.RAIN: Rain can collect as beads on the windshield while you are driving. The wipers clear a path through the drops so you can see the road.

the-family-car-5.solvingTip: Start at 5 Down with where the wrappers go after lunch. Its crossing names what you might have eaten between two pieces of bread at 6 Across.

clues.BIN: Container at the rest area for discarded picnic wrappers
clues.WATER: Clear drink you could pack with a roadside lunch
clues.TABLE: Flat surface where people set a picnic lunch at a rest stop
clues.BREAK: Short pause for food or a stretch along a trip

notes.WATER: At this rest-area picnic, water is the drink taken along with the sandwiches. A packed bottle can be ready even at a stop without a drinking fountain.
notes.TABLE: A rest-area picnic table gives you a surface for food and a map. The bench is the lower part you sit on.
notes.SANDWICH: A sandwich is easy to unpack at a short picnic stop. Its wrapper can unfold on the table and catch crumbs before everything goes back in the bag.

everyday-timekeepers.solvingTip: Find the short word for what you do when the alarm sounds at 10 Across. A crossing leads to the device that makes the sound at 8 Down.

clues.FACE: Front of the clock where you see the numbers and pointers
clues.CLOCK: Timepiece that can be wound and set to ring in the morning
clues.HAND: Moving pointer on the face of an alarm clock

notes.CLOCK: A spring-driven alarm clock is wound to store energy for the movement inside. The alarm can have its own control for setting when it will ring.
notes.HAND: The short hand shows the hour and the long hand shows the minutes. Some bedside alarm clocks have one more pointer to show the time set for the alarm.
notes.HOUR: The hour hand is the shorter pointer on the bedside clock. If you want the alarm to ring at seven, look for the seven when setting its separate pointer.

everyday-timekeepers-2.solvingTip: Look for the time halfway through the day at 10 Across. It crosses the name for a pointer that reaches twelve on the clock face at 9 Down.

notes.NUMBER: The same numbers serve both hands. The short hand uses them to show the hours, while the long hand counts five minutes from one number to the next.
notes.CLOCK: The wall clock's longer hand can be read as minutes around its face. The shorter hand tells which hour those minutes belong to.
notes.HOUR: At exactly noon, the hour hand and minute hand point to twelve. Half an hour later, the short hand is already partway toward one.

clues.NUMBER: Figure such as twelve on the clock face

everyday-timekeepers-3.solvingTip: Begin with the strip that goes around your wrist at 10 Down. Its crossing names the fastener that keeps the strip closed at 11 Across.

clues.BUCKLE: Fastener with a pin that fits a hole in a watch strap
clues.STRAP: One of the leather strips attached to the watch
clues.CLASP: Fastener whose parts snap or hook together on a watch band

notes.BUCKLE: The holes let you choose how loose or tight the watch sits on your wrist. The pin slips into the hole that fits.
notes.WATCH: A wristwatch gives you the time with a glance at its face. On a watch with hands, the short one tells the hour and the long one shows the minutes.

everyday-timekeepers-4.solvingTip: Try the drink made by letting leaves sit in hot water at 2 Down. Its crossing names what you do until the timer sounds at 7 Across.

clues.DIAL: Numbered control you turn to set the kitchen timer

notes.DIAL: Turning the dial sets the number of minutes. As the timer runs, the control moves back toward zero before the bell sounds.
notes.WATER: The hot water draws flavor from the tea leaves. The timer marks how long the leaves or tea bag sit in it.

everyday-timekeepers-5.solvingTip: Find the short word for one dated square at 4 Down. Its crossing names the whole chart you turn to see a new month at 5 Across.

notes.NUMBER: A new calendar page starts with the number one even if the first day falls halfway across a row. The days of the week continue in their usual order while the date starts over.
notes.PAGE: On a flip calendar, turning to the next page reveals the dates in the new month. You can mark an appointment directly on the square for its date.
notes.CALENDAR: One month may end in the middle of a week, and the next starts on the following day. The calendar keeps that order when you turn to the new page.

clues.NUMBER: Mark such as 1 or 15 identifying a day of the month
clues.PAGE: Calendar sheet turned to show a new month

porch-and-patio.solvingTip: Picture the part of the chair where your elbow rests at 6 Down. It crosses the name for a chair that moves back and forth at 7 Across.

clues.ARM: Part of a chair where you rest an elbow
clues.SHADE: Area out of direct sun beneath the porch roof

notes.PORCH: A flat porch floor leaves room for the curved base of a rocking chair to move. The roof overhead can shade the seat on a bright day.
notes.SHADE: The porch roof can cast shade over the rocker even when the steps are sunny. That gives you a cooler place to sit close to the door.
notes.CHAIR: The chair's curved runners let the whole frame rock as you shift your weight. The seat is the part where you sit within that frame.

porch-and-patio-2.solvingTip: Try the word for how it feels out of the hot sun at 2 Across. Its crossing at 2 Down names the cover over the patio.

notes.TABLE: The table is the part of the patio setup that the awning shades from above. The awning's edge can move in or out as you roll it up or extend it.
notes.SHADE: The awning spreads shade across part of the patio. Rolling it in leaves more of the table exposed to the sun.
notes.RAIN: A little rain can run toward the outer edge of a sloped awning. The patio table sits below the covered section, away from most of those drops.

porch-and-patio-3.solvingTip: Find what moves through the mesh when the breeze blows at 2 Down. Then use its crossing for the border that holds the mesh in place at 3 Across.

clues.FRAME: Rigid border that holds the door's mesh in place
clues.SPRING: Coiled piece that helps pull a screen door shut
clues.SCREEN: Mesh stretched inside a summer door's frame

notes.SPRING: Opening the door stretches or twists the spring. When you let go, the stored pull moves the door back toward its frame.
notes.HANDLE: The screen door's handle lets you pull it open without pressing against the mesh. A spring can bring the door back toward the frame.
notes.SCREEN: In a screen door, the screen is the mesh stretched inside the frame. The small openings let air pass through and can block many insects.

porch-and-patio-4.solvingTip: Look for what goes in the pitcher to keep the water cold at 1 Across. Its crossing at 2 Down names what catches drips beneath one glass.

clues.GLASS: Drinking vessel set on a coaster
clues.HANDLE: Part of a serving pitcher you hold to pour a drink

notes.WATER: Water in the pitcher can be cooled with ice and flavored with a slice of lemon. The coaster under a cold glass catches the drops that form on its outside.
notes.HANDLE: A pitcher handle helps you control the tilt when you pour a drink. With a heavy pitcher, the other hand can support the bottom.
notes.TABLE: A patio table holds the pitcher while a tray can carry several glasses from the kitchen. Put coasters down before you set out the cold glasses.

porch-and-patio-5.solvingTip: Try the word for the sound the tubes make when they strike at 5 Down. A crossing leads to what you do when you attach them under the roof at 9 Across.

notes.STRING: A short piece of string can suspend each tube so it moves freely. The ringing starts when a moving part strikes a tube.
notes.PORCH: The porch roof gives the chimes a place to hang. They can catch a breeze along the open edge while staying under cover.
notes.METAL: A metal chime tube vibrates when it is struck. Tubes of different lengths can give different notes in the same breeze.

clues.STRING: Thin cord that holds a wind chime tube up
clues.PORCH: Covered part of a house entrance where chimes may hang
clues.METAL: Material such as aluminum used in some chime tubes

memories-of-schooldays.solvingTip: Find the cover you lift to get inside the lunch pail at 10 Down. Its crossing names the place where the pail sits beside a desk at 9 Across.

notes.SANDWICH: In the old school lunch pail, the sandwich is the main part of the meal. A cookie or an apple can fit beside it without needing another container.
notes.COOKIE: A cookie can fit beside a sandwich as a small treat for the school lunch. Wrapping it separately helps it stay crisp until the lunch pail is opened.
notes.SCHOOL: The school desk is where the lunch pail can wait until the meal break. Its lid keeps the food covered during the lesson.

clues.SANDWICH: Bread and filling packed for lunch in a school pail
clues.COOKIE: Small baked treat that can be tucked into a lunch pail
clues.BREAK: Pause in the school day when a child can eat lunch

memories-of-schooldays-5.solvingTip: Try the short name for the class that deals with numbers at 10 Across. Its crossing at 2 Down asks what each area of study on a report card is called.

notes.TEACHER: A teacher may add a comment beside a grade to explain a strength or a point to work on. The report travels home so the family can see that progress.

clues.TEACHER: Person who may write comments on a report card

memories-of-main-street.solvingTip: Think of the small piece of metal money handed over at the ticket window at 4 Across. Its crossing points to the fabric that can open to reveal the screen at 4 Down.

clues.CURTAIN: Fabric hanging pulled aside when a movie is about to begin
clues.REEL: Round holder that a strip of motion-picture film winds around
clues.WINDOW: Opening in a booth where a movie ticket is sold
clues.NICKEL: Five-cent coin that once bought a movie ticket
clues.SCREEN: Large flat surface where a film is shown

notes.SCREEN: The projector sends light through the pictures on the film. A large flat surface lets people seated around the room see those pictures.
notes.WINDOW: The ticket window is the opening where a customer pays the clerk. The movie screen is deeper inside, where the picture is shown.
notes.NICKEL: Early nickelodeons commonly charged a nickel for admission. That five-cent price helps explain the first part of the name.

memories-of-main-street-2.solvingTip: Start with the clear container that holds loose sweets at 7 Down. Its crossing names the little bit of food you get as something special at 8 Across.

notes.GLASS: Clear jars let customers see which candy is inside. The glass holds the pieces, and the counter is the surface where the shopkeeper sets the jar down.
notes.SWEET: A piece of candy can be sweet whether it melts in your mouth or stays hard while you eat it. At the counter, a scoop can lift several small drops out of the jar at once.
notes.COUNTER: Glass jars can be set on the candy counter so customers can see their choices. A bag can rest on the flat surface while the clerk fills it.

clues.GLASS: Clear material that lets you see inside a candy jar
clues.COUNTER: Raised surface where a candy shop sets its jars

memories-of-main-street-3.solvingTip: Find the coin worth ten cents at 8 Across. Its crossing helps with the numbered wheel you turn on an old telephone at 8 Down.

clues.DIAL: Numbered wheel you turn to enter digits on an old telephone
clues.NICKEL: Five-cent coin an old pay phone might take

notes.RECEIVER: Lift the receiver to hear the other person's voice. The numbered wheel on the telephone is the part you turn when placing the call.
notes.GLASS: The clear panels in a traditional phone booth let people see whether it is occupied. The booth door is what you open to use the phone.
notes.NICKEL: On an old pay phone, a slot might take nickels as well as other coins. The price of a call depended on the phone and the period.

memories-of-main-street-5.solvingTip: Try the toothed tool that pulls through hair at 1 Across. Then look at its crossing for the person who uses it in the shop at 2 Down.

clues.SHOP: Place you go for a haircut
clues.CLIP: Snip a small amount of hair with scissors
clues.CHAIR: Seat a barber can raise or lower during a haircut
clues.POLE: Upright with stripes outside a barbershop

notes.WHITE: A modern American barber pole often has white, red, and blue stripes. The white stripe stays recognizable even when the design is turning behind a clear cover.
notes.CHAIR: A barber's chair can turn and change height so the barber can reach different parts of the head. The striped pole outside helps people find the shop.
notes.POLE: The pole outside a barbershop displays a spiral of colored stripes. Some versions turn, making the stripes seem to climb as the pole spins.

songs-with-everyday-words.solvingTip: Look up in your mind at 10 Across to name what holds the clouds. It crosses the direction of the setting sun at 8 Down.

notes.CLOUD: The song's picture of the open range includes skies that are clear through the day. A cloud would break up that open stretch of sky.
notes.HOME: In the song title, home is where the singer feels at ease. The range is the wide country the singer calls home.
notes.FIELD: A field on the range can be an open stretch of grass. The song's deer and antelope help set that outdoor scene.

clues.CLOUD: White or gray patch in an otherwise clear sky
clues.HOME: Place to live, as in the title about the range
clues.FIELD: Open stretch of ground that can be covered with grass

songs-with-everyday-words-3.solvingTip: Try what you do when you perform a tune with your voice at 5 Across. Its crossing helps with the expression that turns up the corners of your mouth at 2 Down.

notes.LIGHT: Light is something sunshine brings to the scene. A gray cloud can soften it, just as the song title uses sunshine to suggest a brighter feeling.
notes.SONG: A repeated part of a song is sometimes called a refrain. In You Are My Sunshine, the familiar title helps people recognize the part they can join in on.
notes.CLOUD: A gray cloud can make a sunny place look dimmer. That bit of everyday weather helps explain why sunshine in the song suggests being cheered up.

clues.CLOUD: Gray patch that can dim the sunshine

songs-with-everyday-words-4.solvingTip: The bicycle in the title is meant for more than one rider. Try the number at 10 Across, then use its crossing to name what a rider sits on at 8 Down.

clues.SEAT: Part of a bicycle that supports a rider
clues.CHAIN: Linked metal part that moves when the bike is pedaled

notes.WHEEL: A tandem bicycle still has a front and a back wheel. The extra rider has a second seat and pair of pedals between those wheels.
notes.CHAIN: A bicycle chain runs over toothed wheels and carries motion from the pedals to the back wheel. A bicycle built for two can link the two sets of pedals as well.

songs-with-everyday-words-5.solvingTip: Look for the bright object you often see after sunset at 2 Across. Its crossing names the kind of musical piece this title belongs to at 1 Down.

notes.LIGHT: Moonlight is sunlight reflected from the Moon. The word light in the song title refers to that glow on a clear night.
notes.NIGHT: The song title gives the Moon a silvery glow. On a clear night a bright moon can even cast faint shadows.
notes.SONG: This song uses a moonlit evening as the setting for a romantic invitation. The singer can carry that idea through the words and the tune.

classic-movie-settings.solvingTip: Start with the kind of pet Dorothy takes along at 11 Across. Then use its crossing to spell the pet's name at 7 Down.

clues.TIN: Metal in the name of Dorothy's companion who wants a heart
clues.BRICK: One of the yellow blocks in the road Dorothy follows

notes.YELLOW: The road Dorothy follows is yellow. The Emerald City is associated with green, so the two color references point to different places in the film.
notes.BRICK: The film's road is made to look like a long band of yellow bricks. Each block is one small part of the repeated paving you see on screen.
notes.ROAD: The road gives Dorothy and her companions a route to follow toward the Emerald City. The yellow blocks show which way that route goes.

classic-movie-settings-3.solvingTip: Try the smaller rise in the land at 8 Across. One of its letters crosses the place children go for lessons at 5 Down.

notes.SCHOOL: School is one place for lessons. In the musical, Maria can also teach the children during an outing, with singing as part of the lesson.
notes.SONG: A hillside song gives the characters one tune to sing together. Its words and melody are part of the larger musical story.
notes.MUSIC: The music in this scene comes from voices singing on the hillside. The hillside gives the performers room to move while they sing.

classic-movie-settings-4.solvingTip: Find the framed toy that catches the wind at 1 Down. Its crossing names the thin cord you hold on to at 4 Across.

notes.STRING: The kite scene uses string for the line held by the person on the ground. Wind lifts the kite while that line keeps it from drifting away.
notes.FAMILY: Jane and Michael are the children in the family Mary Poppins works for. A nanny's work is caring for the children in the household.
notes.WIND: Here wind is the moving air that lifts a kite. It rhymes with pinned. When you wind the string back onto a reel, the word rhymes with find.

clues.WIND: Moving air that lifts a kite

classic-movie-settings-5.solvingTip: Think of what a traveler might wear on the head at 3 Down. Its crossing asks for the outer garment worn over the shoulders at 5 Across.

clues.LETTER: Travel document in Casablanca, as in a ___ of transit

notes.LETTER: The film's letters of transit are travel papers. They help explain how the story gets from the cafe to the airport.
notes.COAT: Rick wears a coat over his clothes during the farewell at the foggy airport. The coat and hat fit the outdoor scene where the travelers are about to leave.
notes.PIANO: Sam plays the piano in Rick's cafe. Its music is part of the setting, and a song at the piano links the cafe to memories the characters share.

memories-of-home-entertainment.solvingTip: Try the part you turn by hand on the front of an old television at 3 Down. Its crossing names what you hear from the set at 5 Across.

clues.KNOB: Round control turned by hand to adjust an old television
clues.DIAL: Numbered part of the tuner that shows the channel
clues.SET: Another word for the television in the living room
clues.SCREEN: Part of the television where the picture appears

notes.CHANNEL: Turning the tuner selects a broadcast. If the picture is weak, moving the indoor antenna can help the receiver pick it up.

memories-of-home-entertainment-2.solvingTip: Look for the opening at the center of the record at 1 Down. Its crossing names the narrow track the needle follows at 4 Across.

clues.NEEDLE: Small tip on a record player that follows the groove
clues.LABEL: Printed circle at the center of a record showing its title

notes.NEEDLE: The needle rides in a narrow groove in the record. Movement from that groove becomes the sound you hear.
notes.LABEL: The round label at the center of a record can list its song title, artist, and side. The grooves that carry the recording begin farther out from the center.
notes.SPIN: A record spins on a turntable while the needle follows its groove. The record player keeps the disc turning at a steady speed so the music sounds as intended.

memories-of-home-entertainment-3.solvingTip: Find the curved piece of glass that focuses light at 8 Across. Then use a crossing to name the surface where the picture appears at 5 Down.

clues.SCREEN: Flat surface where the projector shows the picture
clues.TRAY: Holder that keeps several slides in order for the projector
clues.LIGHT: What shines through a slide to project a picture
clues.PHOTO: Picture taken with a camera that can be shown from a slide

notes.SCREEN: The projector sends light through one slide at a time. You see a larger version of the picture on the flat surface in front of it.
notes.LIGHT: The projector shines light through the slide. Its lens focuses the enlarged picture on the screen, where it is easier to see in a darkened room.
notes.PHOTO: A slide holds a small transparent photo in a mount. Putting the slides in order in the tray lets the family pictures follow one another during the show.

memories-of-home-entertainment-5.solvingTip: Start with the spool that holds the home movie at 10 Across. Its crossing names the strip that carries the pictures at 9 Down.

clues.PROJECTOR: Device that runs a strip of film to show moving pictures
clues.SPOOL: Holder that takes up the strip after it runs through the projector
clues.FILM: Flexible strip of pictures that runs through a movie projector
clues.REEL: Round holder the rolled-up movie is stored on between showings
clues.CAMERA: Device that recorded home movies on film

notes.FAMILY: A reel of home movies can show milestones in a family's life, from an ordinary outing to a birthday. The pictures appear to move when the reel runs through a projector.
notes.SCREEN: A projector's light puts the family movie on the screen. A flat, pale surface catches that picture so several people can watch it together.
notes.CAMERA: A home movie camera recorded a series of pictures on film. Later, a projector showed those pictures in quick order so the people on the screen seemed to move.

remembering-simple-play.solvingTip: Try the action of pointing toward your target at 2 Down. One crossing leads to the small glass ball you want to send there at 5 Across.

notes.GLASS: Glass marbles can have colored swirls sealed inside them. Their smooth round surfaces let them roll when you shoot one across the ground.
notes.HAND: You can cup a few marbles in the palm of your hand. To roll one toward the circle, hold the others aside and move the one you are using forward with a finger or thumb.

clues.GLASS: Hard material used to make many playing marbles

remembering-simple-play-2.solvingTip: Find what lands inside one chalk square at 7 Across. Its crossing at 4 Down asks what you do to send a marker into another square.

clues.TURN: One player's chance to go through the hopscotch squares
clues.NUMBER: Mark such as 1 or 2 written in a hopscotch square

notes.NUMBER: The numbers show the order to follow on a hopscotch grid. A square with a marker in it is usually the one the player skips when hopping through.

remembering-simple-play-3.solvingTip: Begin with the toy that bounces at 1 Down. It shares a square with the hard material the little game pieces are made of at 6 Across.

clues.TURN: One player's chance to bounce and catch the ball
clues.RUBBER: Springy material used in the ball for jacks

notes.RUBBER: A rubber ball changes shape a little when it hits the floor, then springs back. The time it spends in the air gives the player a chance to pick up jacks.

remembering-simple-play-4.solvingTip: Find the pointed toy that turns in place at 1 Across. Its crossing at 2 Down names what you do to the string to make the toy spin.

clues.POINT: Sharp end the spinning toy balances on
clues.WIND: Wrap the string around the toy before pulling it
clues.STRING: Thin cord wound around a spinning top before pulling

notes.POINT: The toy balances on a small spot where its point touches the floor. When it slows, it starts to lean away from that spot.
notes.COLOR: Color bands on a painted top can look blurred while it spins. When it stops, the separate bands are easier to see.
notes.STRING: Wrapping string around the top lets a quick pull turn the toy. It then balances for a short time on its point.

remembering-simple-play-5.solvingTip: Try the small vessel that stands in front of a doll at 9 Across. A crossing helps name the bigger vessel with a spout at 8 Down.

notes.BASKET: A small basket can hold toy cups while you carry them to the checkered blanket. The blanket becomes the place to set out the pretend meal.
notes.PLATE: The picnic plate is small enough for a doll's meal. Set it on the blanket with the toy cups to make a place setting.
notes.BLANKET: A small checkered blanket gives the doll picnic an outline on the ground. Its squares can help separate the cups from the plates in the pretend place settings.

clues.BASKET: Small carrying container for toy cups
clues.PLATE: Small flat dish for a doll's pretend lunch
clues.BLANKET: Small cloth spread out for a doll's pretend picnic

winter-indoor-afternoons.solvingTip: Picture what you open to read a story at 6 Down. Its crossing names what you pull over your lap to stay warm at 6 Across.

notes.WINDOW: The window is where you can see snow falling from inside the room. A nearby lamp still gives you enough light to read when the daylight fades.
notes.BLANKET: A blanket keeps your lap covered while you hold the book above it. The top edge can be folded down so your hands stay free to turn a page.
notes.SNOW: Snow can pile up outside while a reader stays inside under a quilt. The light beyond the window often looks brighter when the ground is covered.

winter-indoor-afternoons-2.solvingTip: Start with the drink you make by steeping leaves at 1 Down. It crosses the warm vapor that rises from the kettle at 2 Across.

clues.SPOUT: Shaped opening that guides hot water out of a kettle

notes.WATER: When the kettle boils, some of the water turns to steam. In a whistling kettle, the escaping steam makes the whistle sound.
notes.WINTER: In a cool kitchen in winter, the cloud above the kettle can be easy to see. It forms as vapor cools into tiny drops in the air.

winter-indoor-afternoons-3.solvingTip: Look for the container that holds soil by the window at 6 Across. Its crossing describes a flower stem that reaches high above the soil at 7 Down.

clues.BULB: Round plant base that sends up the flower stalk
clues.FLOWER: Bloom near the top of an amaryllis stalk
clues.WINTER: Cold season when an indoor amaryllis can bloom in January

notes.WATER: The amaryllis bulb stores what it needs to begin growing. After growth starts, water in the potting mix helps support the rising stalk and opening flowers.
notes.FLOWER: An amaryllis grows a tall stalk from its bulb. More than one flower can open near the top of that stalk.
notes.WINTER: A potted amaryllis can bloom indoors during winter. It can bring color to a windowsill while outdoor beds are still quiet.

winter-indoor-afternoons-4.solvingTip: Try the short action that puts a puzzle piece into the space shaped for it at 3 Down. Its crossing names the heater beside the table at 6 Across.

notes.WINTER: A winter afternoon can be spent at the puzzle table near the radiator. An empty corner of the table gives you room to sort pieces with straight edges.
notes.CHAIR: At a puzzle table, the chair can be moved to the edge you are working on. Keep the box where you can still see the picture when you change places.
notes.CORNER: On a rectangular jigsaw, a corner piece has two flat sides that meet at a right angle. Look for the four pieces with that shape to mark the outside corners.

clues.CORNER: Part of a jigsaw border where two straight sides meet

winter-indoor-afternoons-5.solvingTip: Find the band at the end of a sleeve at 1 Across. One crossing gives you a letter for the soft fiber the shirt may be made from at 1 Down.

notes.COTTON: Flannel can be made from cotton. Brushing the surface raises fine fibers and gives the shirt a soft feel.
notes.SOFT: Soft describes how the flannel feels against your skin. A shirt can be thick enough for a chilly day and still bend easily when you fold it.
notes.SHIRT: On a button-front flannel shirt, the collar rests around the neck and the cuffs close at the wrists. Those openings can be fastened when the day turns chilly.

clues.COTTON: Plant fiber used to make many flannel shirts
clues.SOFT: Gentle and pleasant to the touch, like a flannel shirt
clues.SHIRT: Button-front top that can be made of flannel

winter-in-the-neighborhood.solvingTip: Look for the footwear you pull on before walking in snow at 7 Down. Its crossing names the part underneath that leaves a mark at 10 Across.

notes.WHITE: On fresh white snow, the different depths of a boot print make its tread pattern visible. A light dusting later can soften the edges of those marks.
notes.PRINT: A boot print can show grooves left by the sole. Fresh flakes, wind, or melting can soften the mark until the pattern is hard to make out.
notes.FOOT: Each boot covers a foot. The mark it leaves in the snow is usually the pattern of the sole, which can show which way the walker went.

clues.WALK: Path where boots leave marks in the snow

winter-in-the-neighborhood-2.solvingTip: Find the body part suggested by a stick at the snowman's side at 3 Across. Its crossing describes the shape of the packed snow at 4 Down.

clues.ARM: Part of a snowman made with a stick at its side
clues.BUTTON: Clothing fastener used for a snowman's chest

notes.WHITE: The body of a snowman usually keeps the white color of the packed snow. A dark button shows up well on that background.
notes.WINTER: The snowman keeps its shape while the weather stays cold. A scarf can lend it some color before a warm stretch of winter weather softens the snow.
notes.BUTTON: A button pressed into the snow can make a dark spot on the snowman's chest. A short row makes it look as though the snowman is wearing a coat.

winter-in-the-neighborhood-3.solvingTip: Begin with what holds the mailbox up from the ground at 1 Across. Its crossing leads to the place you shovel clear so people can walk up at 1 Down.

clues.BANK: Long mound of snow piled beside the road
clues.PATH: Route cleared for walking to the mailbox
clues.POST: Upright piece that holds the mailbox above the ground
clues.LETTER: Written message delivered to a mailbox

notes.BANK: Clearing the walk or road can leave a ridge of snow along its edge. Here, that ridge is near the mailbox.
notes.WHITE: White snow on the ground can partly hide the edge of a driveway. A dark mailbox or post makes a useful marker when you clear the path.
notes.LETTER: The letter is the piece of mail that goes inside the box on the post. A clear path to the box makes it easier to pick up the mail after a snowfall.

winter-in-the-neighborhood-4.solvingTip: Try the word for the place selling the gifts at 10 Across. At 5 Down, its crossing names the clear material you look through to see the display.

notes.WINTER: When daylight ends early in winter, lit shop windows stand out from the street. You can see the toys and gifts from outside after the shops close.
notes.WINDOW: A shop puts its holiday display behind the front window. People on the sidewalk can see the lit toys and gifts even when the door is closed.
notes.STREET: Main Street is the road lined with the shops in this scene. People can follow its sidewalk from one decorated window to the next.

clues.WINTER: Season of cold evenings and many holiday window displays
clues.WINDOW: Glass-fronted opening where a shop displays gifts

winter-in-the-neighborhood-5.solvingTip: Look for what keeps your head warm at 1 Across. Its crossing names the curved support it can hang from after you come inside at 1 Down.

notes.WINTER: Hang the hat and mittens where air can reach them after a winter outing. Set the pair together so both mittens are there the next time you go out.
notes.WARM: Warm here describes how the hat and mittens feel when worn. Letting the wool dry before the next outing helps it feel comfortable again.
notes.SNOW: Snow caught on a mitten can melt when you come indoors. The wool may feel damp even after the white flakes have disappeared.

clues.WARM: Comfortably heated, as your hands can feel in wool mittens
clues.SNOW: Frozen flakes that melt on mittens indoors

winter-light-and-ice.solvingTip: Find the short word for water in its hard, frozen form at 11 Across. A crossing leads to the season when you may see it on the porch roof at 7 Down.

clues.POINT: Narrow end of an icicle farthest from the roof
clues.WINTER: Cold season when icicles may hang from a roof

notes.POINT: The broad end is nearest the roof. The thin end hangs below it and may drip when the air warms.
notes.WINTER: On a winter day, sun can melt snow on the roof. An icicle can grow when some of that runoff freezes again at the colder edge.
notes.SUN: Sun can warm an icicle enough to start a drip, even while much of the porch stays in shade. The drop forms at the hanging tip before it falls.

winter-light-and-ice-2.solvingTip: Try the word for one flat piece of window glass at 6 Down. Then use its crossing to name the repeated design that frost leaves on the glass at 6 Across.

clues.FEATHER: Bird covering whose shape a frost pattern can resemble
clues.PATTERN: Design made by ice crystals on a windowpane

notes.FEATHER: As the ice grows, small branches can reach outward from a central line. The pattern may look like part of a bird's feather.
notes.WINTER: In winter a window can get cold enough for moisture to form ice crystals on the pane. As the crystals spread they can make patterns like feathers.
notes.PATTERN: One frost patch may branch from a single line, with a second patch starting somewhere else on the glass. Where the two patches meet, the patterns can run together.

winter-light-and-ice-3.solvingTip: Look for the little string that feeds the flame at 9 Down. Its crossing names the season when afternoon light fades early at 10 Across.

notes.WINTER: Winter daylight can fade while it is still afternoon. A nearby candle gives a small warm glow and can cast moving shadows as the flame flickers.
notes.CANDLE: When the candle is lit, a little pool of melted wax can form around the wick. The solid wax around that pool gives the light its shape.
notes.FLAME: A candle flame can lean or flicker in moving air. That motion can make the shadow on the wall shift as well.

clues.CANDLE: Wax light that burns on a wick
clues.FLAME: Flickering part of a fire at the tip of the wick

winter-light-and-ice-4.solvingTip: Find the source of light above the street at 5 Across. One crossing helps with the word for a single piece of snow that catches that light at 3 Down.

clues.LAMP: Light fixture high above the street

notes.LAMP: A streetlamp lights just part of the air around it. Falling flakes may brighten as they pass through that spot.
notes.LIGHT: The streetlamp illuminates a small part of the street. A flake can glow briefly as it passes through that patch of light.
notes.WINTER: Under a streetlamp, winter snow can seem to appear as it enters the beam. Flakes outside that bright patch are much harder to see.

winter-light-and-ice-5.solvingTip: Start with the narrow walking route at 3 Across. Its crossing points to the little pool beside it with a frozen surface at 3 Down.

notes.WATER: The top of a shallow puddle can freeze while water below remains liquid. The first layer at the surface is the thin ice described in the puzzle.
notes.WINTER: A winter puddle may stay frozen longer in the shade. The thin ice can start to melt in parts of the path that get afternoon sun.
notes.PATH: The path is the regular walking route beside the puddle. If the water stays at the edge, there may still be dry ground down the middle.

clues.WATER: Liquid that freezes to make the top of a puddle
clues.WINTER: Cold season when puddles can freeze over
clues.PATH: Walker's route beside the frozen puddle

christmas-sharing-projects.solvingTip: Try the small label that carries a wish at 2 Down. Its crossing leads to the short word for a plaything someone might donate at 2 Across.

notes.RIBBON: A ribbon can decorate the wrapped present. The tag carries the requested gift information, so place it where it stays visible.
notes.CHRISTMAS: An Angel Tree is one way people organize Christmas gift donations. The tag can give details that help a shopper choose a requested gift.
notes.ANGEL: Angel is part of the name Angel Tree, a Christmas giving project. A paper angel or wish tag on the tree can stand for a gift that someone has requested.

clues.ANGEL: Figure that can mark a donation request on a Christmas giving tree

christmas-sharing-projects-2.solvingTip: Find the metal container that keeps the cookies together at 4 Across. It crosses the word for something given to a friend at 3 Down.

notes.RIBBON: Tie the ribbon around the closed tin to dress it up as a gift. The paper inside separates layers of cookies.
notes.CHRISTMAS: Cookies packed in a tin are easy to share at Christmas. The liner between layers helps keep the tops of the cookies tidy until the tin is opened.
notes.COOKIE: A gift tin can hold several kinds of cookies. Firmer ones can sit at the bottom so more delicate shapes at the top are easier to lift out whole.

clues.RIBBON: Decorative strip tied around a gift tin

christmas-sharing-projects-3.solvingTip: Try the tool that puts ink on the envelope at 4 Down. A crossing helps name the little piece of postage added before mailing it at 2 Across.

notes.ENVELOPE: Compare the name on each Christmas card with the name on its envelope before sealing it. That helps the personal greeting reach the person you wrote it for.
notes.STAMP: Putting a stamp on each addressed envelope is one of the last steps before mailing Christmas cards. A check mark on the list can show which ones are ready.
notes.ADDRESS: A holiday card list lets you check each address before it is copied. If a friend has moved, the list gives you one place to record the new street or ZIP code.

clues.ENVELOPE: Folded paper holder used to send a holiday card
clues.STAMP: Postage label you put on a Christmas card's envelope

christmas-sharing-projects-4.solvingTip: Look at 8 Across for the part of a carol you could hum. Its crossing names the single piece of paper people read the words from at 7 Down.

notes.CHRISTMAS: At a Christmas sing-along, a printed carol sheet gives everyone the same words. A pianist can start the tune while guests find the first line.
notes.SHEET: One printed sheet can carry several verses of a carol. A clear title at the top helps guests find the right words before the singing begins.
notes.PIANO: A pianist can give a singer the starting note and keep time as the carol continues. People following a printed sheet can join in once they recognize the tune.

clues.SHEET: Piece of paper printed with the words to sing

christmas-sharing-projects-5.solvingTip: Try what holds one piece of paper to another at 4 Down. Its crossing names the tiny bits that catch the light on a decoration at 4 Across.

notes.TABLE: The craft table gives each person room to make something. Shared scissors or glue can sit in the center where several people can reach them.
notes.PAPER: Thin paper folds easily into a small ornament. A heavier sheet gives a greeting card enough stiffness to stand when folded in half.
notes.RIBBON: On a handmade decoration, a short ribbon loop can also be the hanger. A strip set flat on a card can mark a border.

clues.TABLE: Raised surface where friends set out craft supplies

christmas-little-traditions.solvingTip: Find the front part of the stocking at 9 Down, where a small treat might settle. It crosses the name of the holiday at 8 Across.

notes.FRUIT: An orange is a piece of fruit that fits in the toe of a stocking. Its peel keeps the sections inside until someone is ready to eat it.
notes.CHRISTMAS: An orange can nestle at the bottom of a Christmas stocking because the toe widens there. Small nuts or wrapped treats can fit in the space above it.
notes.COIN: A coin is small enough to tuck beside the orange in a stocking. A bright coin can be a small gift to save after the fruit is eaten.

clues.COIN: Metal money piece small enough to tuck in a stocking

christmas-little-traditions-2.solvingTip: Look for one metal bar the toy wheels run along at 2 Down. Its crossing helps name what goes around the tree at 3 Across.

clues.RAIL: One metal bar that the wheels of the model train run along
clues.WHEEL: Round part that rolls along a toy train track
clues.TREE: Evergreen with a trunk and branches that can be decorated for Christmas
clues.TRAIN: Engine and cars going around a toy track

notes.CHRISTMAS: A toy train set at Christmas can make a loop around the base of the tree. From the front, you may see the engine disappear behind the trunk and come back into view.
notes.WHEEL: Small wheels support the toy engine and cars on the rails. On a curved track, those wheels follow the rails around the tree.
notes.TREE: An evergreen Christmas tree has needles along its branches. If it is a cut tree, a stand at the base holds the trunk upright.

christmas-little-traditions-3.solvingTip: Start with the wavy bend in a piece of candy at 4 Down. Then use its crossing to name the holiday when this candy often appears at 4 Across.

notes.SWEET: Ribbon candy is bent into curves while it is warm and pliable. After it hardens, its sweet taste remains in each thin fold.
notes.RIBBON: In ribbon candy, ribbon describes the shape of a thin strip of sugar candy. The strip is bent into folds before it cools and hardens.
notes.CHRISTMAS: Ribbon candy is often set out at Christmas in several bright colors. A shallow bowl lets more of the thin curls show, since the pieces can be fragile when piled up.

clues.RIBBON: Long, flat strip whose shape a folded Christmas candy copies

christmas-little-traditions-4.solvingTip: Try the little object that rings when the door moves at 9 Across. Its crossing names the light ringing sound you hear at 3 Down.

notes.HANDLE: A ribbon can loop around a round knob or be tied onto a lever handle. Tying it close to the door leaves the end of the handle clear to use.
notes.RIBBON: A ribbon loop suspends the bell from the door handle. When the door moves, the hanging bell can swing and ring.
notes.METAL: The small bell can be made of brass, a kind of metal. Its body rings as it vibrates after the piece inside strikes it.

clues.HANDLE: Part of the door you hold to open it
clues.METAL: Hard material a bell can be cast from

christmas-little-traditions-5.solvingTip: Look at 10 Across for the paper item you wear on your head. Its crossing at 8 Down asks for the word for a little present.

clues.CRACKER: Paper table favor that makes a snap when pulled apart
clues.CHRISTMAS: December holiday when people may pull paper crackers at dinner

notes.PAPER: In this holiday custom, people pull on the ends of a paper cracker. Inside there may be a folded hat, a joke, or a small toy.
notes.PLATE: In a Christmas place setting, a cracker can sit beside the dinner plate. The cracker opens to reveal the folded paper crown.
notes.CHRISTMAS: Pulling crackers at Christmas dinner is especially familiar in Britain. A meal with paper crowns on the guests can be a sign that the crackers have already been pulled.

christmas-preparing-the-room.solvingTip: Try the green part beside a holly berry at 2 Down. It crosses the wax decoration that gives light to the table at 1 Across.

notes.PLATE: The plates go in front of the diners along the sides of the table. The holly and runner are in the middle, where they leave the place settings clear.
notes.CHRISTMAS: Holly gives the Christmas table a mix of green leaves and red berries. The narrow runner brings those colors down the center between the place settings.
notes.CANDLE: A candle on the table gives off light that can catch on nearby plates. The holly decorating the runner belongs well clear of the flame.

clues.PLATE: Dish set in front of each diner on the decorated table
clues.CANDLE: Wax light set in a holder at dinner

christmas-preparing-the-room-2.solvingTip: Find what you do with ribbon to secure it at 8 Down. A crossing helps name one thin green part of an evergreen branch at 9 Across.

notes.BRANCH: A few overlapping evergreen branches can make a continuous garland. The stair rail is the fixed support that holds the greenery up.
notes.RIBBON: The ribbon can add color between the evergreen branches. A separate tie can hold the garland in place on the rail.

clues.BRANCH: Evergreen limb that can be tucked into a garland
clues.RIBBON: Decorative strip you can tie among evergreen branches

christmas-preparing-the-room-3.solvingTip: Look for the pointed decoration placed at the top of the tree at 5 Down. It shares a square with the name of the holiday at 7 Across.

clues.SILVER: Shiny gray color an ornament can have
clues.POINT: Part that sticks out from the center of a star ornament
clues.STAR: Pointed ornament placed at the top of a Christmas tree

notes.POINT: Each point sticks out from the center of the ornament. The tips give it the outline you see above the tree branches.
notes.BRANCH: The branches support the ornaments that hang lower on the tree. The star goes at the top, where the tree narrows to its highest point.
notes.CHRISTMAS: A star on a Christmas tree can recall the star in the Nativity story. Some homes use an angel or another ornament at the top instead.

christmas-preparing-the-room-4.solvingTip: Try the curved piece that holds the ornament to a branch at 1 Down. Its crossing names the small circle at the top of the ornament at 4 Across.

clues.LOOP: Small closed circle at the top of an ornament for hanging
clues.GLASS: Fragile material used for some shiny tree ornaments
clues.HANG: Suspend an ornament from a branch

notes.GLASS: A thin glass ornament can break if pressed against a hard object in the box. Tissue keeps the ornaments from knocking against one another.
notes.CHRISTMAS: When unpacking a Christmas bauble, look for the small loop at its top. A hook or ribbon goes through the loop to hang the ornament from a branch.
notes.HANG: To hang a bauble, slip its hook over a branch that can hold it. Leave enough room between ornaments so the glass won't knock against the next one.

christmas-preparing-the-room-5.solvingTip: Find the part that covers one of the tiny houses at 9 Down. Its crossing names the route between rows of buildings at 8 Across.

notes.CHRISTMAS: In a tabletop Christmas village, several tiny buildings make one street scene. Place taller houses toward the back so smaller shops can be seen from the front of the mantel.
notes.HOUSE: A tiny house in the mantel scene can have a door, lit windows, and a pitched roof. The houses stand beside models of shops or other town buildings.
notes.STREET: A street in the mantel village can be a narrow strip left open between the little buildings. Lining up their front doors along it makes the scene look like a town block.

clues.CHRISTMAS: December holiday celebrated with miniature village displays
clues.HOUSE: Model of a home in a miniature holiday village
clues.STREET: Road that runs between the tiny houses of a model village

thanksgiving-small-moments.solvingTip: Start with the word that identifies the guest at 11 Across. Its crossing names the tool you use to write it at 10 Down.

notes.TABLE: A name card sits at each person's place on the table. Folding the card lets it stand up so the name is easier to read.
notes.PAPER: Choose paper stiff enough to hold a fold. A simple fold in the middle makes a small tent with a place for the name on the front.
notes.FAMILY: Several family members at Thanksgiving may share a last name. A first name or a familiar nickname on a place card makes it easier to find the right setting.

thanksgiving-small-moments-2.solvingTip: Try the word for good fortune at 7 Across. Its crossing names one of the parts a person holds after the bone breaks at 4 Down.

clues.FORK: Place where the turkey bone splits into two branches
clues.PIECE: One part that comes away when a wishbone breaks
clues.TWO: Number of ends people pull on a wishbone

notes.FORK: Each person holds one branch of the wishbone for the traditional pull. The fork is the place where those branches join.
notes.PIECE: Each person holds a branch of the wishbone. When the bone breaks, each has a piece and looks to see which one came away larger.

thanksgiving-small-moments-3.solvingTip: Look for the curved shape of the harvest basket at 4 Across. Its crossing names the small fruit that grows in bunches at 3 Down.

notes.BASKET: A cornucopia is a basket shaped like a horn. It rests on its side so you can arrange fruit and nuts at its wide opening.
notes.TABLE: The Thanksgiving table holds both the meal and the decoration. A cornucopia can sit sideways in the center so its fruit and nuts show through the wide opening.

clues.BASKET: Woven container that can be shaped like a horn

thanksgiving-small-moments-4.solvingTip: Find the action that sends the football to a teammate at 5 Across. Its crossing names the number of points shown during the game at 6 Down.

clues.FIELD: Marked stretch of grass or turf where the game is played
clues.BALL: Oval object the players run with or throw
clues.GOAL: Word before line for the front edge of a football end zone

notes.SCORE: The numbers on the screen tell how many points each team has. The game clock shows how much time remains.
notes.WATCH: To watch a game on TV is to follow what happens on the field from home. A replay lets you see a pass or catch again after the live play is over.

thanksgiving-small-moments-5.solvingTip: Try what holds the whole cheesecake in the oven at 1 Across. One crossing leads to the flat dish used to serve a slice at 1 Down.

clues.PAN: Metal container that holds the cheesecake while it bakes
clues.CHEESE: Cream ___, a main ingredient in the filling
clues.CREAM: First word in the name of the soft dairy ingredient used for cheesecake
clues.CRUST: Firm baked base that holds the cheesecake filling

notes.SWEET: Sugar makes the filling sweet, while cream cheese can give it a slight tang. The pumpkin and spice supply much of the flavor you smell as you take a bite.
notes.CHEESE: Cream cheese gives the cheesecake filling its soft, thick base. The pumpkin mixture is baked on the crust and firms up further as it cools.
notes.CREAM: Here cream is the first word in cream cheese. That soft cheese gives the pumpkin filling a smooth base, while the crust is made separately.

garden-friendly-flowers.solvingTip: Picture what you would scoop around the pansy roots at 2 Down. Follow that crossing to the round dish on the front step at 5 Across.

clues.BOWL: Deep round dish that can hold a few pansies
clues.YELLOW: Bright color often seen near the middle of a pansy bloom

notes.COLOR: Purple and yellow can appear on the same pansy. In the bowl on the step, the blooms may repeat those hues in different combinations.
notes.YELLOW: On a pansy, a patch of yellow near the middle can stand out between dark markings that give the bloom a face-like look.
notes.PETAL: A pansy petal can have a dark patch or several fine lines pointing toward the middle. Those markings help give the bloom its face-like look.

garden-friendly-flowers-2.solvingTip: Look for the buzzing visitor that moves from one zinnia to the next at 7 Across. Its crossing asks what you planted before any flowers came up at 6 Down.

clues.ORANGE: Zinnia color between red and yellow

notes.COLOR: A zinnia's color is easiest to see on the small petals around the center. The green stalk can look much the same on a red flower and an orange one.
notes.PETAL: What looks like a zinnia petal is a broad part of a little flower along the edge. Several rows of those outer flowers can make a zinnia look very full.
notes.STEM: The green stem supports the zinnia flower. When you cut a few for a bunch, leaving some stem below each bloom gives you something to hold or put into a vase.

garden-friendly-flowers-3.solvingTip: Enter the yard through the movable part of the fence at 2 Across. Where it crosses 1 Down, picture one of the white pieces around a daisy's center.

notes.YELLOW: On a familiar white garden daisy, the yellow part is in the center and the white rays spread around it.
notes.WHITE: On many daisies, the parts we call white petals are the rays around a cluster of tiny flowers in the center.
notes.PETAL: The white rays of a daisy usually spread out from the center in a ring. As the bloom ages, they can droop while the yellow center remains on the stem.

clues.PETAL: One white part spreading outward from a daisy's center

garden-friendly-flowers-4.solvingTip: Think of the everyday object that gives an open spring flower its shape at 2 Down. The crossing at 4 Across asks for the flower itself.

notes.SPRING: Tulip bulbs are often planted in fall for flowers along the path in spring. The leaves usually show above the soil before the flower stalks rise.
notes.SOIL: The tulip bulb rests below the top of the soil. Water can drain through loose soil around the bulb while its roots grow downward.
notes.BLOOM: A tulip bloom opens into a cup when its petals spread. When the flower is viewed from above, the center can be seen inside that cup.

clues.SPRING: Season when many tulips bloom along a walk
clues.SOIL: Earth around the bulbs of tulips
clues.BLOOM: Open tulip flower with petals shaped like a cup
clues.WALK: Paved way leading to a front door

garden-friendly-flowers-5.solvingTip: Imagine fastening a climbing stem loosely to its support at 10 Down. Use the crossing letter to name the shape of the leaves at 9 Across.

notes.FLOWER: Many familiar morning glories open early in the day. The open blue flower has a different shape from the heart-shaped leaves along the vine.
notes.SEED: A morning glory can start from a seed planted near a fence. As the young vine grows, its stem can wind around the support.
notes.FENCE: A morning glory can twine around the narrow parts of a fence. An open fence also leaves the leaves and flowers easy to see from either side.

clues.FENCE: Yard barrier a vine can climb

garden-cutting-table.solvingTip: Find what you would stand the cut flowers in at 12 Across. Then look at 11 Down for the part you'd shorten to make a flower sit lower.

notes.COLOR: A single snapdragon stalk can have open blossoms and unopened buds at the same time. Look at the open blossoms for the clearest view of their color.
notes.GLASS: In a clear glass vase, you can see the water line and the cut ends of the snapdragon stems. The taller blossoms and buds sit above the vase's narrow neck.
notes.BLOOM: The lower blossoms on a snapdragon often open first. A stem can carry open blooms down low with unopened buds still near the tip.

clues.GLASS: Clear material a tall vase can be made of
clues.BLOOM: One open flower on a tall snapdragon stem

garden-cutting-table-2.solvingTip: Picture suspending the lavender upside down at 2 Down. Its crossing at 3 Across asks for a spot out of direct sunlight.

notes.STRING: The string keeps the lavender stems together as they dry. Leaving a loop above the knot gives you something to hang the bundle from.
notes.FLOWER: A lavender stem carries a cluster of tiny flowers near its tip. Those clusters can keep some of their scent after the cut stems have dried.
notes.DRAWER: A drawer is one place to put dried lavender after it has hung to dry. Keep the flowers in a small bag so loose pieces stay away from the folded clothes.

clues.DRAWER: Pull-out compartment where a bag of dried lavender may be kept

garden-cutting-table-3.solvingTip: At 4 Across, look for the lip that guides water when you pour. The crossing at 5 Down names the whole jug holding the hydrangeas.

notes.WHITE: Some hydrangeas have white clusters when they first open and develop a pink tint as the blooms age. The handled pitcher holds the whole cut stems.
notes.HANDLE: One hand can grip the loop on the side of the pitcher to carry it. The spout is the shaped lip on the opposite side.
notes.PORCH: The porch roof can shade the pitcher from strong sun. Set it where the flower clusters can be seen from the steps without getting in the way of the door.

clues.WHITE: Color of many hydrangea blooms when they first open

garden-cutting-table-4.solvingTip: Start with the wide-mouthed container on the table at 4 Down. At the crossing, 5 Across, fit the two-word name of the fragrant flowers it holds.

notes.WATER: The jar is a vase for ornamental sweet peas. The cut ends of the stems sit in water below the blossoms.
notes.PETAL: A sweet pea has a broad upper petal that can look like a tiny sail. Smaller petals cluster below it, giving the blossom its folded shape.

clues.WATER: Liquid that keeps cut stems fresh in a jar

garden-cutting-table-5.solvingTip: Find the place to sit near the peony at 3 Across. Then think of what you might notice in the air there at 2 Down.

notes.LEAF: A peony's green leaves grow along the stems below its round blooms. The leaves can still fill the space beside the seat after the flowers drop their petals.
notes.PETAL: Full peony blossoms may have several crowded layers of petals. Those layers make the center harder to see, even when the flower is open.
notes.SCENT: Some peonies have a scent you can notice beside the garden seat. The strength of the fragrance can vary even among blooms that look similar.

clues.SCENT: Fragrance you might notice beside a peony

garden-flower-seasons.solvingTip: Start with the still water beside the iris at 8 Down. Follow the crossing toward the clue about one colorful part of a blossom at 8 Across.

clues.CLUMP: Group of stems growing close together
clues.GREEN: Color of the long leaves below an iris bloom

notes.GREEN: The upright leaves can stay green after the iris flowers fade. Their long shape makes the plant recognizable beside the pond even between blooms.
notes.PETAL: Many irises have three upright petals with three broader parts bending down around them. That gives the bloom a different outline when you look at it from the side.
notes.SPRING: Many garden irises flower in spring or early summer. In this scene the blooms rise along the pond edge while their long leaves form a clump below.

garden-flower-seasons-2.solvingTip: Find the little building where you keep garden tools at 7 Down. Its crossing asks for the tall flower growing beside the wall at 8 Across.

notes.FLOWER: Hollyhock flowers line the tall stalk, and the lower ones often open first. From the side, you can see buds higher up above the open blooms.
notes.SUMMER: Hollyhocks can bloom along the shed wall in summer. Since the buds open over time, the same tall stalk can have both unopened buds and flowers.
