notes.SEED: Hollyhock seeds can form in small round cases after the flowers fade. Collect them once those cases turn dry and brown.

clues.FLOWER: Bloom that opens along a hollyhock stalk
clues.SEED: Small part that can be saved from a dried flower head for planting

garden-flower-seasons-3.solvingTip: Imagine how those long flower stems move in a gentle wind at 6 Down. Use the crossing to name the warm season at 6 Across.

notes.FLOWER: What looks like one cosmos flower has many tiny flowers crowded into the center. The broad outer parts give the bloom its daisy-like shape.
notes.LIGHT: In this scene, light describes the force of the breeze. It is gentle enough to make the top of a cosmos stem sway a little.
notes.SUMMER: Cosmos can keep flowering through summer and into early fall. The flowers rise above fine leaves, so you can see them sway even when the lower foliage is still.

clues.LIGHT: Mild in force, as a gentle breeze

garden-flower-seasons-4.solvingTip: At 4 Across, find the part of the planter the petunias spill over. The crossing at 3 Down asks how the stems hang down its side.

notes.FLOWER: A petunia has a flared, trumpet-shaped flower at the end of a stem. On trailing kinds, several blooms can hang past the planter's rim.
notes.SUMMER: Trailing petunias can bloom through much of summer. As the stems grow past the rim, some flowers turn to face away from the sides of the planter.
notes.SOIL: The petunias' roots grow into the soil inside the planter. Their stems can then trail beyond the rim while the base of each plant stays in place.

garden-flower-seasons-5.solvingTip: Picture a snowdrop with its opening facing the ground at 5 Across. Name the ringing object it resembles, then cross into the clue for an open flower at 5 Down.

notes.WHITE: Look for the white hanging bloom above the snow or bare soil. Some snowdrops have small green marks on the inner parts of their flowers.
notes.GREEN: On a snowdrop, most of the bloom is white. Look closely toward the center and you may see small green marks above the hanging tips.
notes.SPRING: Snowdrops can bloom in late winter, before many other bulbs have opened. Their small hanging flowers are an early sign that spring is near.

clues.WHITE: Usual color of a snowdrop flower
clues.SPRING: Season many snowdrops signal as winter ends
clues.LEAF: Narrow green part that grows beside a snowdrop flower

needle-and-thread-projects.solvingTip: Think of how you secure the end of a sewing thread at 1 Down. The crossing at 4 Across names the small fastener you're putting back on the sweater.

clues.SPARE: Extra button kept in case one falls off
clues.SCISSORS: Two-bladed tool used to trim sewing thread
clues.THREAD: Thin strand used to sew a button back on

notes.SCISSORS: Use scissors to cut a fresh length of sewing thread. After you tie the final knot behind the button, trim the loose end close to it.
notes.THREAD: Choose thread that blends with the button or the sweater. Passing it through the holes more than once can help hold the button in place.
notes.BUTTON: A spare button can replace one that fell off the front of the cardigan. Hold it opposite the right buttonhole before taking the first stitch.

needle-and-thread-projects-2.solvingTip: Look at the turned-under bottom of a curtain at 11 Down. Its crossing at 10 Across asks for the measurement you adjust by sewing it higher or lower.

notes.WINDOW: Measure from the curtain rod to where you want the bottom to sit near the window. The hem sets that lower edge after the fabric is folded under.
notes.THREAD: Thread can be chosen to match the curtain fabric so the hem is hard to see from the front. The stitches hold the turned edge in place.
notes.NEEDLE: A fine needle can catch a little of the outer curtain fabric and then pass back into the fold. That is one way to make a hem with stitches that barely show on the front.

clues.THREAD: Thin strand that can hold a curtain hem in place

needle-and-thread-projects-3.solvingTip: Picture the little curve of cord that slips over a fastener at 4 Down. Follow it to the round fastener itself at 6 Across.

notes.SCISSORS: Scissors cut the felt to size before it is folded. Rounded corners can be trimmed into the soft fabric before the case is stitched together.
notes.THREAD: Strong thread can hold the felt at the edges of a needle case. A different color can leave a visible line of stitches around the cover.
notes.NEEDLE: The felt keeps the needles from sliding around loose. Slip each needle point into an inner layer so you can see and grasp the other end when the case opens.

clues.NEEDLE: Small pointed sewing tool that can be tucked inside a felt case

needle-and-thread-projects-4.solvingTip: Start with a little piece left in the sewing basket at 3 Down. Its crossing at 7 Across asks what you could sew and stuff with a few of those pieces.

clues.PINCUSHION: Small stuffed pad that holds pins and needles
clues.COTTON: Plant fiber used in cloth scraps for a pincushion

notes.COTTON: A tightly woven cotton scrap can form the outside of the pincushion. Sew the pieces together around the edge so the filling stays inside.
notes.STITCH: Close stitches keep the stuffing from working through the edges of the pincushion. Small, evenly spaced loops can make the two fabric pieces sit smoothly together.
notes.THREAD: Sew around most of the pincushion and leave a gap for stuffing. Keeping enough thread on the needle lets you close that gap after the cushion is filled.

needle-and-thread-projects-5.solvingTip: Find the round frame that keeps the napkin flat while you sew at 10 Across. At the crossing, 6 Down names the material stretched inside it.

clues.LETTER: One of the symbols in the alphabet
clues.CORNER: Point where two edges of a cloth napkin meet
clues.STITCH: One small pass of the needle in a sewn letter

notes.COTTON: Cotton cloth can stay flat in an embroidery hoop while you sew. The hoop gives the napkin corner enough tension for small stitches.
notes.CORNER: A napkin corner is easy to spot even when the napkin is folded. Leave a little space between the initial and each of the two nearby edges.
notes.STITCH: Several short stitches placed end to end can trace the shape of a letter. The line can curve if you make the stitches shorter around the bend.

yarn-for-useful-things.solvingTip: Use the clue at 1 Down for making fabric with two needles. Where it crosses 5 Across, think of the band a different color of yarn makes.

notes.STITCH: A knit stitch forms when new yarn is drawn through a loop on the needle. Repeating that motion across a row builds up the striped scarf.
notes.NEEDLE: The knitting needle holds the loops in order as you work across the scarf. Starting the new color at an edge makes the color change fall between full rows.
notes.LOOP: The loop on the needle is an opening the yarn can pass through when you form another stitch. Keeping each loop about the same size makes an even row.

clues.STITCH: Single loop of yarn worked with a knitting needle
clues.LOOP: Opening made by a bend in yarn on the needle

yarn-for-useful-things-2.solvingTip: Start at the basin where the dishcloth will get used at 3 Across. Its crossing at 3 Down takes you back to the small loop you made with the hook.

clues.CHAIN: A row of linked loops made with a crochet hook
clues.HOOK: Curved tool used to pull yarn through loops
clues.STITCH: One small loop made with a crochet hook
clues.COTTON: Plant fiber spun into yarn for many dishcloths
clues.ROW: One line of stitches worked across the dishcloth

notes.CHAIN: The first linked loops in crochet can form the starting edge of a dishcloth. Later stitches are worked into those loops.
notes.COTTON: Cotton can be spun into yarn for a dishcloth. It takes up water, and the finished square can be rinsed and washed after use.
notes.STITCH: A crochet stitch is made with the hook and yarn. Keeping the loops about the same size helps the dishcloth grow into an even square.

yarn-for-useful-things-3.solvingTip: Think of the warm fiber that comes from sheep at 2 Across. Then use its crossing for the fluffy decoration you can make for the top of a hat at 1 Down.

clues.SCISSORS: Two-bladed tool for trimming the ends of yarn
clues.STRING: Thin cord tied around the middle of a pom-pom

notes.STRING: The tie at the middle holds the pom-pom together when the loops are cut. A long end of that tie can also help attach it to the hat.
notes.SCISSORS: Cut through the loops of yarn after the middle is tied. Then use the scissors to trim the loose ends round without cutting the center tie.

yarn-for-useful-things-4.solvingTip: Imagine sitting down and spreading a blanket over your thighs at 9 Across. The crossing at 7 Down asks for one of the long tools used to make its loops.

clues.ROW: Line of stitches across the knitting
clues.PATCH: Small piece of fabric sewn over a worn spot
clues.STITCH: One worked loop in a knitted row
clues.BLANKET: Soft knitted covering for your lap

notes.STITCH: A lap blanket grows one stitch at a time across each row. The stitches along the sides are especially easy to see when the blanket lies flat.
notes.BLANKET: A lap blanket can be shorter and narrower than a bed blanket. That size lets it cover the thighs and knees while leaving the feet clear of most of the hanging cloth.
notes.NEEDLE: A wide lap blanket may need longer needles or a pair joined with a flexible cord. That leaves room for more loops than you would hold when making a narrow scarf.

yarn-for-useful-things-5.solvingTip: Find the loose bit you would catch to start winding at 4 Across. Its crossing names the loose bundle you are unwinding at 2 Down.

clues.BALL: Round bundle formed by winding yarn
clues.LOOP: Curved opening formed by a loose strand of yarn

notes.COLOR: Use the yarn color as a quick way to tell the wound bundles apart. Loose ends can be tucked under a few strands to keep the balls from unwinding.
notes.LOOP: A loose length of yarn can form a loop as you wind the ball. Straighten stray loops as you go so the yarn unwinds more easily when you use it.

paper-for-keepsakes.solvingTip: Think of what's waiting on your nightstand at 7 Down. The crossing at 7 Across asks for the card you can slip inside to find your place tomorrow.

notes.COLOR: The card stock and the tassel can be different colors. A tassel that shows up against the cover makes it easier to find the marker in a closed book.
notes.PAPER: Card stock is thicker than ordinary writing paper, so the finished bookmark stays fairly flat. A hole near one end leaves room for a tassel.
notes.PAGE: Slip the bookmark beside the page where you plan to start reading again. Leave the tassel outside the book so you can lift it without thumbing through the pages.

clues.PAGE: Numbered side in a book where a marker can go

paper-for-keepsakes-2.solvingTip: Begin with the picture you took at a picnic at 3 Across. Where it crosses 1 Down, find the point where two edges of that picture meet.

notes.SCISSORS: Scissors can trim a caption or backing sheet to fit the scrapbook page. A printed copy of the picnic photo can be trimmed to fit the space above it.
notes.CORNER: Small paper photo corners can slip over the points of a picture. They hold the picture on the page while leaving the center clear.
notes.PHOTO: A scrapbook photo can sit next to a caption about the picnic. A date or park name adds details that may be hard to recognize later from the picture itself.

clues.SCISSORS: Tool with two blades for trimming scrapbook paper
clues.CORNER: Point where two edges of a photo meet
clues.PHOTO: Camera picture you can mount on a scrapbook page

paper-for-keepsakes-3.solvingTip: At 12 Across, look for the little label that tells who gets the present. Its crossing at 8 Down names what you can thread through the opening and tie.

clues.STAMP: Tool pressed in ink to print a small design
clues.HOLE: Opening punched through the tag for string
clues.STRING: Thin cord that passes through a gift tag's hole
clues.RIBBON: Decorative fabric strip used to dress up a gift tag

notes.STRING: Put the string through the punched hole before you tie on the label. The name and other ink marks go on the stiff paper itself.
notes.RIBBON: A ribbon is wide and flat enough to make a small bow on the tag. The thin string can pass through the hole to hold the tag to the gift.
notes.SCISSORS: Use scissors to cut the tag from stiff paper. A hole punch can make a small round opening for the string near one end.

paper-for-keepsakes-4.solvingTip: Think of the folded paper object you could wave on a hot day at 4 Across. The crossing at 1 Down takes you to the part you grip.

notes.COLOR: The paper's color still shows in the fold valleys. On a sheet printed on just one side, the reverse can also show when the fan is opened.
notes.HANDLE: The paper pleats open above the handle. The handle gives your fingers a place to grip without squeezing the wide part closed.
notes.FOLD: Fold the paper forward and then backward, keeping the folds about the same width. The alternating bends let the fan open wide at the top.

clues.FOLD: Bend paper to make one of a fan's pleats

paper-for-keepsakes-5.solvingTip: Start with the container that keeps your mementos together at 4 Down. The crossing at 5 Across asks for a picture you might save in it.

notes.RIBBON: A strip of ribbon can make a border around the lid of the memory box. It can be glued down so the lid still lifts without untying anything.
notes.PAINT: Paint can go on the outside of the memory box and around its edges. Let the painted lid dry before closing it or attaching the decoration.
notes.LETTER: A saved letter can carry a memory in the writer's own words. Keeping a letter with a photo from the same occasion gives both items more context.

clues.LETTER: Handwritten message someone might save in a keepsake box

painting-home-projects.solvingTip: Start with the part that keeps rain out of the bird shelter at 7 Down. Where it crosses 8 Across, think of the material you cut into boards to build it.

clues.PERCH: Small bar a bird can rest on
clues.SAND: Smooth the wood by rubbing it with rough paper
clues.BRUSH: Bristled tool for painting the outside of a birdhouse

notes.COLOR: On a wooden birdhouse, the color comes from the paint coating the wood. The wooden perch is the small bar where a bird can land.
notes.PAINT: On a wooden birdhouse, paint can color the outside walls and roof. The inside can be left bare for the nesting birds.
notes.BRUSH: A small brush reaches the joints where the birdhouse walls meet the roof. A wider one can cover the flat side of the box more quickly.

painting-home-projects-2.solvingTip: Picture the top lip of a clay flower container at 9 Down. Use the crossing at 10 Across to name what you brush on to add color.

clues.SEAL: Coat the painted surface to keep moisture out
clues.PAINT: Colored coating a brush can put on a clay pot

notes.COLOR: Terra cotta usually has a reddish-brown color before it is painted. The painted marks form the pattern over that clay background.
notes.PAINT: Paint can be dabbed onto a clay pot in dots or short strokes. A firm surface under your brush helps keep the marks in the pattern you want.
notes.PATTERN: A row of dots or small marks can form a pattern around the pot's rim. Leaving similar gaps between marks makes the design easier to follow around the curve.

painting-home-projects-3.solvingTip: Think about what the stones have to be before you can paint them at 3 Down. The crossing at 4 Across takes you back to washing off loose dirt with clean water.

clues.FLOWER: Blossom shape you might paint on a garden rock
clues.STONE: Small piece of rock that can be painted for the garden

notes.COLOR: Damp stones may look darker than dry ones. Wait until a rinsed stone dries to see how its natural color looks next to the paint.
notes.FLOWER: In this craft, a flower can be a painted design on the stone. A center dot and a few shapes around it can make the design recognizable.
notes.STONE: A flat stone has a broad spot for the design and will rest steadily on the ground. A bump at the edge can make a small painted line harder to follow.

painting-home-projects-4.solvingTip: Picture touching the brush lightly to the opening in a stencil at 7 Down. Where it crosses 9 Across, find the sticky strip that holds the stencil in place.

clues.REPEAT: Make the same stenciled shape again
clues.PAINT: Colored liquid dabbed through the openings of a stencil
clues.BRUSH: Bristled tool used to dab paint through a stencil

notes.COLOR: Using a different color on the border can make a stenciled design easier to see. Wait for the first paint to dry before repositioning the stencil.
notes.PAINT: Apply the paint with a light dab through the stencil. A brush carrying a lot of wet paint can push it under the edge and blur the shape.
notes.BRUSH: A stencil brush can have short, firm bristles with a flat end. That end can tap straight down through the opening and leave the cutout shape on the tray.

painting-home-projects-5.solvingTip: Find what you would apply with a wet brush at 9 Across. The crossing at 6 Down names the small handled object you're trying to capture on paper.

clues.SHADE: A lighter or darker form of a color
clues.WASH: Thin coat of watercolor spread with a wet brush
clues.PAINT: Coloring material you apply to paper with a wet brush

notes.SHADE: Compare the shaded side of the cup with the side facing the light. On paper, painting the darker side can make the cup look round.
notes.HANDLE: In a side view of a teacup, the handle usually has a small open space between the loop and the cup. Leaving that opening clear helps the grip read as a separate shape in a painting.
notes.PAINT: Watercolor paint spreads more thinly when you add water to it. Let an early layer dry before adding a sharper line around the cup.

beads-and-ribbons.solvingTip: Look for the little pierced piece of jewelry at 8 Across. Its crossing at 4 Down names a fine strand you could pass through the opening.

notes.GLASS: Glass is what some of the beads are made from. Beads of different colors can use the same material, while a hole through each bead lets you thread it.
notes.THREAD: Beading thread passes through the holes as you make the bracelet. Leave some extra at the ends to fasten the clasp.

clues.GLASS: Hard material made into some colored beads
clues.THREAD: Fine strand that can pass through bracelet beads

beads-and-ribbons-2.solvingTip: Think of the decoration made by tying two loops at 9 Across. Use its crossing to work out the narrow piece of fabric they're made from at 6 Down.

clues.TAIL: One of the ribbon ends left loose below a bow
clues.SCISSORS: Two-bladed tool for trimming ribbon ends

notes.RIBBON: Pinching the ribbon at the center gives you a place to tie the loops together. The loose ends below the knot are the tails of the finished bow.
notes.SCISSORS: Scissors make a clean cut at each ribbon end. If you cut the tails at an angle after tying the bow, you can compare how they hang first.

beads-and-ribbons-3.solvingTip: Picture the small opening drilled through a bead at 3 Down. The crossing at 4 Across names the material the beads were made from.

notes.COLOR: The beads can all be the same shape and still make a pattern. Alternating light and dark beads is a pattern made by color alone.
notes.STRING: The string has to fit through the holes in the wooden beads. If a bead has a large hole, the knot at the end needs to be big enough to hold it in place.
notes.PATTERN: Beads can repeat in groups of shapes, such as two small round beads followed by a larger one. The repeated order is still visible when the strand is worn.

clues.PATTERN: Repeated order of shapes or colors along a strand of beads

beads-and-ribbons-4.solvingTip: Find the little decoration you slide onto a cord at 9 Across. The crossing at 7 Down asks for the opening the cord passes through.

notes.COLOR: A row of bright beads can help you pick your keys out of a bag. A bead's color describes how it looks, while the knot in the cord keeps it from sliding off.
notes.THREAD: A fine thread can pass through holes too small for a thick cord. Doubling the thread is one way to make the strand stronger if both strands still fit.
notes.CORD: A cord is a thicker strand that can go through the holes of larger beads. Tie it to the metal ring to hold the beaded part together with the keys.

clues.THREAD: Thin strand that can pass through small holes in beads
clues.CORD: Thicker strand that can hold beads on a key ring

beads-and-ribbons-5.solvingTip: Find the soft container you're making at 10 Down. Its crossing at 9 Across asks for the narrow fabric strip that will make the carrying loop.

clues.RIBBON: Narrow fabric strip that can form a bag handle
clues.HANDLE: Ribbon loop you hold when carrying the bag
clues.STITCH: One pass made with a needle to fasten ribbon to cloth
clues.THREAD: Thin strand used to sew a ribbon handle to cloth

notes.HANDLE: The ribbon loop serves as a handle once both ends are stitched to the bag. The middle of the loop stays free for your fingers.
notes.STITCH: Stitches across the ribbon end attach it to the cloth bag. A second row can share the pull when you lift the bag by the ribbon.
notes.THREAD: The thread goes through both the fabric and the end of the ribbon. A close color match can make those stitches blend into the ribbon.

easy-woodwork-projects.solvingTip: Imagine what collects as you smooth the wood at 5 Across. The crossing at 6 Down takes you to the flat surface you're making to store things.

clues.DUST: Fine dry particles left after sanding
clues.RUB: Move sandpaper back and forth against wood

notes.SHELF: The front edge of a wooden shelf is often the part you touch as you reach for something. Sanding in the direction of the grain helps smooth that edge.
notes.CORNER: The shelf corner is where two cut edges meet. Light sanding can soften a sharp point there so it feels smoother to the touch.

easy-woodwork-projects-2.solvingTip: Picture one wall of the wooden box at 1 Down. Where it crosses 4 Across, think of what extra water needs to do after you water the plants.

notes.SEED: A planter holds soil around the seed. Drainage lets extra water escape from the box, leaving air in some of the spaces between bits of soil.
notes.SOIL: Leave the soil a little below the rim of the wooden box. That space gives water room to soak in before it reaches the top edge.
notes.SCREW: A screw can join the side of the planter box to an end board. Its thread grips the wood across the joint when both pieces are brought together.

clues.SOIL: Loose growing material you put in a planter box
clues.SCREW: Threaded fastener used to join boards on a planter box

easy-woodwork-projects-3.solvingTip: Start with the toothed tool you use to cut the frame pieces at 5 Across. Follow the crossing at 2 Down to the clear material that goes over the picture.

notes.GLASS: The pane is fitted behind the wooden edges and in front of the picture. Its job is to protect the picture while letting you see it.
notes.CORNER: At each frame corner, the ends of two pieces meet. Cutting both ends at matching angles lets the joint make one clean right angle.
notes.FRAME: A frame made for a picture needs an opening sized to let the image show. A narrow part of the wood overlaps the picture's edge to hold it in place.

clues.CORNER: Point where the angled ends of a picture frame meet

easy-woodwork-projects-4.solvingTip: At 2 Down, find the flat item with a raised edge. The crossing at 3 Across asks what its two handles help you do.

clues.SAND: Rub a rough wooden surface to make it smooth
clues.SCREW: Threaded fastener that can attach a handle to a tray

notes.HANDLE: A tray's two handles let you lift from both sides. Holding one in each hand helps keep the base level as you carry it.
notes.PAINT: Paint can collect along the edges of the tray if a coat is too thick. A thin coat makes it easier to keep the edges smooth as it dries.
notes.SCREW: A screw can fasten each handle to the wooden tray. Once its head is seated, the handle should stay in place as the tray is lifted.

easy-woodwork-projects-5.solvingTip: Find the short pin that sticks out of a coat rack at 2 Down. At the crossing, 3 Across asks what you'd do with your coat when you come in.

notes.SCREW: Screws can attach the back of a peg rack to the wall. The pegs stick out for the coats while the fasteners hold the board in place.
notes.LEVEL: A level can show whether the peg rack runs straight along the wall. Checking it before the screws are set helps keep the pegs in an even row.
notes.HANG: Hang a coat by slipping its inside loop over a peg. The peg carries the coat's weight while the sleeves hang freely below.

clues.SCREW: Threaded fastener that can hold a peg rack on a wall
clues.HANG: Put a coat on a peg so it dangles

quiet-table-hobbies.solvingTip: Think of the outside boundary you're assembling first at 8 Down. The crossing at 7 Across asks for one of the small parts that goes into it.

notes.TABLE: Spread the jigsaw pieces flat on a table so their edges are easy to compare. A corner piece normally has two straight sides.
notes.PIECE: Shape helps you place each piece, and so does the small part of the picture printed on it. Once the border is together, pieces with no straight edges fit inside it.
notes.BOX: The puzzle box can hold the pieces you have yet to sort. Its lid often shows the full picture, which helps you tell similar parts of the border apart.

clues.TABLE: Flat piece of furniture where you can spread out a jigsaw
clues.PIECE: Single part of a jigsaw that fits next to others
clues.BOX: Container that often shows the finished jigsaw on its lid

outdoor-hobby-bags.solvingTip: Find the long pencil mark you could make across the paper at 10 Across. The crossing at 9 Down takes you to the seat you might draw, or sit on, at the park.

clues.SHADE: Darken part of a drawing with a pencil
clues.PENCIL: Pointed drawing tool that can make erasable lines
clues.ERASER: Small tool for rubbing away an unwanted pencil line in a sketch

notes.SHADE: Light pencil strokes can show the gray areas of a drawing. A soft stroke leaves room to darken an area later.
notes.PENCIL: The pencil's point makes a narrow line for an edge in the sketch. Tilting the pencil can bring the side of the point against the paper for a wider mark.
notes.ERASER: An eraser can lift a faint guide line before you darken a sketch. Light pressure helps spare the nearby strokes you want to keep.

outdoor-hobby-bags-2.solvingTip: At 10 Across, find the long pole you hold while fishing. Follow it to the crossing at 9 Down for the artificial bait you might tie onto the line.

clues.LINE: Thin cord that connects the rod to the bait
clues.HOOK: Curved pointed piece that catches a fish

notes.LINE: Fishing line runs from the reel through the guides on the rod. The end can carry a lure or a baited hook.

outdoor-hobby-bags-3.solvingTip: Think of the protective holder for your binoculars at 8 Across. Where it crosses 4 Down, look for the kind of book you'd open to identify a bird.

clues.BINOCULARS: Handheld viewer that makes distant birds look closer
clues.TREE: Tall woody plant a birdwatcher may look up into
clues.WALK: Outing on foot to look for birds

notes.TREE: A tree gives you a place to start looking with binoculars. Follow the trunk up toward the branches and look for a bird's outline against the open sky.
notes.WING: A wing folded against a bird's body may show bars or patches of color. With binoculars, those marks can help you tell similar birds apart.
notes.FEATHER: When a bird moves its wing, you may see feather markings that were tucked out of sight. Binoculars help you compare the shape and color of those marks.

outdoor-hobby-bags-4.solvingTip: Look for the transparent piece the light enters through at 11 Across. Its crossing at 6 Down takes you to the control you press when the flower is in view.

clues.FRAME: Decide what to include inside the edges of a photo
clues.LIGHT: What a camera lens lets in to make a photograph
clues.CAMERA: Device you aim to take a garden photo

notes.BUTTON: On many cameras, pressing the shutter button partway sets the focus. Pressing it the rest of the way takes the photo.
notes.LIGHT: The camera lens gathers light from the flower and the rest of the scene. The shutter controls when that light reaches the film or sensor.
notes.CAMERA: The camera makes the photograph once the flower is in the frame and in focus. Check the edges of the view for anything you want to leave out.

outdoor-hobby-bags-5.solvingTip: Find the toy you fly on a line at 1 Down. The crossing at 5 Across asks for the long strip trailing from it in the air.

clues.FRAME: Stiff support that holds a kite in shape
clues.TAIL: Long strip trailing behind a kite
clues.STRING: Line you hold while a kite flies

notes.COLOR: A dark or bright color can help you keep track of a paper kite against the sky.
notes.STRING: String links your hand to the kite's frame. The tail is a separate strip that trails behind the kite.
notes.PAPER: The paper forms the light surface across the kite frame. The frame keeps that sheet stretched out so moving air can lift it.

collecting-family-stories.solvingTip: Picture turning a family photo over at 9 Across. Where it crosses 7 Down, think of the information tag you could attach so the names stay with the picture.

notes.FAMILY: A family photo may hold several generations in one picture. Names written together with an occasion can help someone later work out how those people knew one another.
notes.LABEL: A photo label can record which person stands on which side of a group picture. The back of the print has room to write those details away from the image.
notes.PHOTO: Look at the people, clothes, or background of an old photo when placing it in order with others. A later label can record what you were able to work out.

clues.LABEL: Tag or written note identifying people in a picture

collecting-family-stories-2.solvingTip: Start with the stiff slip you pull from the kitchen box at 1 Across. The crossing at 2 Down asks for the cooking directions written on it.

clues.DISH: Prepared food such as a casserole
clues.FAMILY: Relatives who may pass recipes down through generations
clues.BOOK: Bound pages where family recipes can be kept

notes.FAMILY: A family recipe book can hold dishes passed between generations. A note about who made a dish can keep part of its story with the instructions.
notes.BOOK: A family recipe book can hold both handwritten instructions and notes. Leaving a margin near the binding gives you room to keep a page open while you read.
notes.DATE: A date written on a recipe card can show when the recipe was copied or used. It can also help place that card among others in the book.

collecting-family-stories-3.solvingTip: Find the brief reminder you might write before an interview at 11 Across. At the crossing, 7 Down asks what to do while your grandparent is telling the story.

clues.RECORD: Save someone's voice so you can play it back later
clues.VOICE: Sound of a person speaking that a recorder can capture
clues.LISTEN: Pay attention while a grandparent tells a story

notes.VOICE: A recording keeps the sound of the grandparent's voice along with the words. Pauses and changes in tone can carry details that are harder to put on a page.
notes.NAME: Saying a name at the start of the recording can identify the storyteller for anyone who listens later. A place or date can be added if it helps set the scene.
notes.LISTEN: Listen for details in the grandparent's story that you can ask about next. A pause after the question gives the person time to remember before answering.

collecting-family-stories-4.solvingTip: Think of the word for your mother's or father's sister at 6 Across. It crosses 5 Down, the word for either your mother or your father.

clues.BRANCH: Part of a family tree that traces one line of relatives

notes.BRANCH: In a family tree, one branch might show your aunt and her children. Another branch might show your own household.
notes.FAMILY: A family tree shows how people are related across generations. Placing siblings on the same level makes it easier to see which people share a parent.
notes.PARENT: On a simple family tree, put the parent on the level above the child. A line between them shows the relationship at a glance.

collecting-family-stories-5.solvingTip: Find the metal container where the keepsakes are stored at 6 Across. The crossing at 3 Down asks for the mailed message you could unfold from inside it.

notes.RIBBON: Tie a ribbon loosely around a small stack of letters to keep them together in the tin. You can lift out the stack without having to gather each letter from the bottom.
notes.LETTER: An old letter can show a date and a signature in the person's handwriting. Those details can help identify it when several letters are stored together in the tin.
notes.STAMP: A stamp on an old envelope can give a keepsake letter some history. The separate postmark over it may show a date even if the letter inside is undated.

clues.LETTER: Written message saved with others in a keepsake tin
clues.STAMP: Postage label that can be saved on an old envelope

flower-and-fabric-crafts.solvingTip: At 11 Down, think of fastening the little bag shut with ribbon. The crossing at 10 Across asks what you notice when you open the drawer.

notes.FLOWER: Dried flower heads or buds give the sachet its scent. The little fabric bag keeps the pieces together in a drawer.
notes.RIBBON: The ribbon draws the top of the little bag shut and can make it easy to open again. The seam is the line of stitches that holds the cloth together.
notes.NEEDLE: The needle carries the thread through both pieces of cloth at the edge of the sachet. Close stitches help keep small dry flowers inside.

clues.FLOWER: Blossom dried for a scented cloth bag
clues.NEEDLE: Pointed tool that carries thread through a cloth pouch

flower-and-fabric-crafts-2.solvingTip: Find the plant part you're laying between pages at 8 Down. Use its crossing at 9 Across to name one of the branching lines still visible after pressing.

notes.PAPER: Place plain absorbent paper on either side of the leaf. It takes up some moisture and helps protect the printed pages of the book.
notes.LEAF: A pressed leaf shows its outline and the lines of its veins after it has dried. Some of the original green may fade to brown.
notes.BOOK: A closed heavy book can press a leaf between protected pages. Its weight spreads across the leaf to help the edges dry without curling.

clues.PAPER: Absorbent sheet material used to press leaves
clues.LEAF: Part of a plant you can press flat and dry between pages
clues.BOOK: Bound pages you can close over a leaf to press it flat

flower-and-fabric-crafts-3.solvingTip: Look for the circular base of the wreath at 10 Across. The crossing at 7 Down asks for one narrow length of fabric you can tie onto it.

notes.COLOR: Repeating two fabric colors around the ring makes a pattern even if all the strips are cut to the same size.
notes.COTTON: Cotton cloth can be cut into short strips for the wreath. Their cut edges may fray a little, giving the tied ring a softer look.
notes.SCISSORS: Fabric scissors let you cut along a line in cotton cloth. Narrow strips fit closer together as you tie them around the ring.

clues.SCISSORS: Tool with two blades for cutting cloth strips

flower-and-fabric-crafts-4.solvingTip: Think of the line where the pieces of the cushion cover meet at 3 Across. Its crossing at 3 Down asks for one small loop of thread along that line.

clues.COVER: Removable fabric case that fits over a cushion
clues.THREAD: Fine strand used to sew the edges of a cushion cover together
clues.SOFT: Easy to press down, like a filled cushion

notes.STITCH: Stitches run along the edges of the cloth to make the cover. Once the cushion is inside, the seam sits at the edge where two pieces of fabric meet.
notes.THREAD: Thread can be chosen to match the cushion cover fabric. It still joins the two pieces along the edge, even when the seam is hard to see.
notes.SOFT: The cushion feels soft because the filling gives under light pressure. The cover fits around that filling and keeps it together in one shape.

flower-and-fabric-crafts-5.solvingTip: Picture securing the paper around the gathered stems at 4 Down. The crossing at 3 Across takes you back to what you did with the scissors to trim them.

notes.COLOR: Plain wrapping paper leaves the flowers as the strongest color in the bunch. The scent is the part of the bouquet you notice by smell.
notes.PAPER: The paper wraps around the cut stems so the bunch can be carried together. Leave the flower heads above the open top of the wrapper.
notes.FLOWER: The bouquet is the whole group of cut flowers. One flower has its own head, with a stem below it to hold or trim.

bible-beginnings.solvingTip: Think of what you might see overhead in the dark at 3 Across. Follow its crossing to the time named for the darkness in the creation story at 4 Down.

notes.NIGHT: In Genesis 1, the darkness is named Night and the light is named Day. The names appear near the beginning of the creation account.
notes.FRUIT: Genesis 1 describes trees bearing fruit with seeds in it. The fruit is part of the growth described after dry land appears.

clues.NIGHT: Name given to darkness in the opening of Genesis

bible-beginnings-2.solvingTip: Start with the name of the garden where Adam and Eve lived at 11 Across. The crossing at 9 Down asks for the kind of waterway that flowed out of it.

notes.FRUIT: The Eden account names the tree connected to the fruit. The kind of fruit is left open in Genesis.
notes.GARDEN: In Genesis, the garden is the place where Adam is put to work and care for what grows there. The story names Eden as the surrounding place.
notes.RIVER: The river in the Eden story flows out to water the garden. Genesis describes it dividing into four branches farther on.

clues.FRUIT: Food from a tree in the Eden story
clues.GARDEN: Place in Eden where Adam was put to tend what grew

bible-beginnings-4.solvingTip: Picture the bird that brought a leaf back to Noah at 3 Down. Its crossing at 6 Across asks for the tree the leaf came from.

notes.WATER: In Genesis, the flood waters recede before the dove brings back a leaf. The rainbow appears later as a sign of God's promise.

clues.WATER: What rose during the flood in Noah's story

bible-beginnings-5.solvingTip: Find one of the building blocks used at Babel at 8 Down. Its crossing names the tall structure the people built with those blocks at 10 Across.

notes.BRICK: Genesis says the builders made bricks and fired them hard. Those blocks are what they use for the city and tower.
notes.TOWER: The people in the Babel story plan a tower that reaches high into the sky. The tower is one part of the city they set out to build.

clues.BRICK: Building block the people of Babel made and fired

bible-family-journeys.solvingTip: Start with Abraham's fabric shelter at 11 Down. Then look at 10 Across for what he offered his visitors to wash their feet.

notes.WATER: In Genesis 18, Abraham offers his visitors water to wash their feet. The meal and the place to rest are other parts of the welcome.
notes.SHADE: In Genesis, Abraham offers travelers a place to rest under a tree. The branches give them shade while food is prepared.

clues.WATER: What Abraham offered his visitors to wash their feet

clues.JUICE: Sweet liquid that can come from sliced berries
clues.SPRING: Season when early local strawberries may reach a market

spring-house-and-yard.solvingTip: Think about the condition the boots should be in before they go into storage at 4 Down. The crossing at 5 Across asks what you call two matching ones.

clues.BRUSH: Bristled tool for removing dried mud from boots
clues.WINTER: Coldest season, when boots help keep feet warm
clues.LACE: Cord loosened to open a boot

notes.WINTER: The boots go into storage when winter ends. Brushing dirt from the soles and letting the pair dry helps keep the inside of the box clean.
notes.BRUSH: A boot brush can work around seams where dried grit sticks. Clearing that grit from the edge of the sole helps keep the closed storage box clean.
notes.LACE: Boot laces run over the front of the ankle. Loosening them lets you pull the tongue forward so air can reach farther inside before the boots go into the box.

spring-house-and-yard-2.solvingTip: Find the action that blends the contents of the tin before you start at 8 Across. Its crossing at 6 Down names what you'll spread on the porch rail.

clues.POST: Upright support for a porch rail
clues.PORCH: Raised area outside a door, often bordered by a rail
clues.BRUSH: Bristled tool for applying paint to a porch rail

notes.PORCH: A porch rail runs along the exposed edge or beside the steps. The posts hold it up while you scrape away the old paint and apply a fresh coat.
notes.BRUSH: A narrow brush can reach the places where the porch rail meets its posts. After spreading paint along the top, look underneath for drops that have collected along the lower edge.

spring-house-and-yard-3.solvingTip: At 10 Across, look for one flat section of the window you're washing. Use the crossing to name the long mark you want to remove from it at 6 Down.

clues.FRAME: Border that holds a window in place

notes.FRAME: The window frame surrounds the opening in the wall. A pane is one flat piece of glass in the window.
notes.GLASS: The glass is the smooth surface under the rubber blade. The frame holds it, and marks can collect where the pane meets that frame.
notes.WINDOW: A window can still show a faint mark after the wash water dries. Looking across the glass from one side can help you see streaks that disappear when you face it squarely.

spring-house-and-yard-4.solvingTip: Think of what you do to secure the pad to the chair with its strings at 9 Down. The crossing at 10 Across asks for the paved area where you set the chairs out.

clues.CUSHION: Soft pad you can tie to a patio chair
clues.CHAIR: Outdoor seat that can hold a tied cushion

notes.PORCH: The patio is where the cushions can sit in the sun. The covered porch gives you somewhere to move them if a shower comes along.
notes.SHADE: A bright patch can help warm the damp cushions. Moving into shade later lets you sit outside without the sun falling directly on the chair.
notes.CHAIR: Some chairs have a place on the frame to tie on the cushion. The ties keep the pad from sliding when you get up from the seat.

spring-house-and-yard-5.solvingTip: Start at the entrance panel that holds the decoration at 1 Across. The crossing at 2 Down asks for the narrow strip of fabric you could arrange in a bow.

notes.BASKET: This kind of basket is part of the decoration. A hanging loop or handle lets it sit upright on a hook while the twigs and flowers show above the rim.
notes.FLOWER: Twigs help fill out the door basket and can hold the flowers in place. Position the blooms where they will show above the rim.
notes.SPRING: A spring door basket can use bare twigs left from winter with a few fresh blooms. The branches show the change from bare wood to new growth.

clues.BASKET: Container hung on a door to hold flowers and twigs

spring-garden-wildlife.solvingTip: Think of a familiar sky color when you picture the eggs at 11 Down. Its crossing at 10 Across takes you to the bird that laid them.

notes.BRANCH: A robin can build its nest where two sturdier branches meet. Smaller pieces of grass and twigs go into the nest itself.
notes.GRASS: A robin can use grass stems with twigs to build a nest. Fine dry grass can line the cup where the eggs rest.
notes.SPRING: Spring is a common time to see an American robin nesting. The parent may sit low over the eggs so the blue shells are tucked out of sight.

clues.GRASS: Narrow-leaved growth a robin can use to line a nest
clues.SPRING: Season when many robins build nests and lay eggs

spring-garden-wildlife-2.solvingTip: Start with the short springing movement a frog makes at 11 Across. At 7 Down, think of what happens to the water when the frog lands in it.

notes.BANK: At a pond, the bank is where dry ground meets the water. Frogs often sit near that edge.
notes.NIGHT: At night it can be easier to hear the frogs without seeing them. The call might be coming from the bank or from reeds at the edge of the pond.
notes.GREEN: Some frogs near a pond have green patches that blend with the reeds. Their skin can also have darker marks or spots.

spring-garden-wildlife-3.solvingTip: Think of how the bumblebee gets from one blossom to another at 4 Across. Its crossing at 3 Down names the powder that can stick to it along the way.

notes.TREE: In an apple tree, fruit can develop from blossoms after pollination. A bee may move between blossoms as it visits the tree.
notes.APPLE: As a blossom develops into an apple, its petals fall away. A little dried remnant of the bloom can often be seen at the end opposite the stem.
notes.SPRING: Apple trees bloom for a short stretch in spring. On a warm day during that window, you can often hear bees moving between the blossoms.

clues.TREE: Woody plant that can hold many apple blossoms
clues.APPLE: Round fruit with a core that starts as a blossom on a tree
clues.SPRING: Season when apple blossoms open before fruit grows
clues.FUZZ: Soft hair covering a bumblebee's body

spring-garden-wildlife-4.solvingTip: Look for the small unopened growth a leaf can come from at 7 Down. The crossing at 7 Across asks for the tree limb supporting it.

notes.BRANCH: A branch can have several buds along it. When the buds open, each one can send out a few new leaves.
notes.LEAF: A new leaf can be soft and folded when it first comes out of the bud. It spreads out as it grows along the branch.
notes.SOFT: Young leaves can feel soft and bend easily when they first unfold. As a leaf matures, it can become firmer along its edges and veins.

clues.LEAF: Thin green part that unfolds from a tree bud
clues.SOFT: Tender and easy to bend, like a new leaf

spring-garden-wildlife-5.solvingTip: Picture the part of a butterfly that opens and closes as it flies at 9 Down. Its crossing at 11 Across asks for the time of year when the first warm days arrive.

notes.FLOWER: A butterfly can uncurl a long feeding tube to reach nectar inside a flower. The bloom gives it a place to land while it feeds.
notes.INSECT: A butterfly is an insect even when it spends a long time resting. It has six legs, although some kinds hold their front pair close to the body.
notes.SPRING: Some butterflies that spend winter sheltered as adults can appear right away on a warm spring day. A sunny spot gives them a place to rest and warm up.

summer-neighborhood-days.solvingTip: Start with the utensil you eat the icy dessert with at 3 Down. The crossing at 5 Across asks for a rounded serving of a frozen treat.

notes.SWEET: Lemon ice can be sweet and sour in the same spoonful. Sugar softens the tartness of the lemon without making the citrus flavor go away.
notes.SUMMER: At a summer street fair, a frozen lemon ice can soften quickly in the sun. Its small cup catches what melts while you eat it with a spoon.
notes.LEMON: Lemon juice can give the frozen treat its tart flavor. Some versions also use a little finely grated outer peel for its scent.

clues.LEMON: Citrus fruit used to flavor an icy fair treat

summer-neighborhood-days-2.solvingTip: Think of what you do with your hands after the last song at 1 Down. Where it crosses 3 Across, find the raised area where the musicians played.

notes.CHAIR: A folding lawn chair comes along for the outdoor concert. Set it where you can see and hear the performers without blocking the walk behind you.
notes.SONG: At a lawn concert, a band can play several songs during one set. A pause at the end of a song gives the audience a place to clap.
notes.MUSIC: The music on the lawn is played live for people sitting nearby. One tune can be carried by the trumpet while the rest of the band plays along.

clues.CHAIR: Seat you might bring to an outdoor concert
clues.SONG: Words and a tune that performers can present at a lawn concert

summer-neighborhood-days-3.solvingTip: Find the flexible tube you connect to the sprinkler at 9 Across. The crossing at 7 Down asks what all that water helps grow on the lawn.

notes.WATER: A hose brings water to the sprinkler. The sprinkler breaks that flow into many drops and spreads them over a wider part of the lawn.
notes.GRASS: The grass is what the sprinkler waters across the lawn. Watching where the drops land helps you see which part is still dry.
notes.RAINBOW: The sprinkler makes its own curtain of drops. When the sun is behind you and the angle is right, those drops can show a small rainbow close to the grass.

clues.RAINBOW: Colored arc sometimes seen in sprinkler spray

summer-neighborhood-days-4.solvingTip: At 8 Down, think of the gentle back-and-forth motion you feel on the porch. The crossing at 9 Across asks for the part your weight rests on.

clues.CUSHION: Soft pad on a porch swing
clues.SWAY: Move slowly from side to side or back and forth
clues.SUMMER: Warm season when you can sit out late on a porch
clues.SWING: Hanging porch seat that rocks back and forth
clues.CHAIN: Line of metal links that holds a porch seat up

notes.SUMMER: A summer evening can stay warm after the porch falls into shade. The hanging seat can still sway a little after your feet stop pushing.
notes.SWING: A gentle push with your feet can set the porch swing moving. Its wide seat gives two people room to sit side by side if the swing is made for it.
notes.CHAIN: A porch swing's chains support the seat from above. Their links move at the hooks as the seat rocks back and forth.

summer-neighborhood-days-5.solvingTip: Find the tough green outside of the melon at 7 Down. The crossing at 10 Across asks for one of the little things you might pick out of the juicy red part.

clues.RIND: Tough outer skin of a watermelon
clues.SWEET: Sugary in taste, as the red part of a ripe watermelon can be
clues.WEDGE: Piece of watermelon with a wide rind edge

notes.SWEET: The red part of a ripe watermelon often has the sweetest taste. Near the green rind, a paler layer can taste milder.
notes.SUMMER: Watermelon is a familiar picnic fruit in summer. Leaving the rind on a wedge gives you something to hold if you eat it outside without a plate.
notes.WEDGE: A watermelon wedge usually has a curved strip of rind along its wide side. That firm edge gives you something to grip while eating the soft fruit.

summer-away-from-home.solvingTip: Think of what you can dry off with after swimming at 9 Across. At its crossing at 4 Down, look for the patch out of the sun under the umbrella.

clues.UMBRELLA: Wide cover on a pole that shades beach chairs
clues.SHELL: Hard covering from a sea animal, sometimes found washed up on a beach

notes.SUMMER: On a sunny summer beach, an umbrella's patch of shade moves during the day. The chairs can be shifted closer to the pole if the shade moves away from them.
notes.SHADE: The umbrella puts a patch of shade on the sand. Both chairs can share it if they sit close enough to the pole.
notes.SHELL: A shell washed onto a beach can have ridges spiraling around the opening. That shape gives you a clue that it may have come from a sea snail.

summer-away-from-home-2.solvingTip: Find the tree with needles near the lake at 4 Down. Its crossing at 5 Across asks for the small vacation house it grows beside.

notes.WINDOW: A cabin window can open toward the lake. A screen across the opening lets the breeze through and keeps many insects outside.
notes.CHAIR: A chair near a cabin window or on the porch can give you a view of the dock. The dock itself is the platform you cross to reach a boat.
notes.SCREEN: The cabin screen fits between the open window and the outdoors. If it can be taken out of the frame, that makes it easier to clean dust from the mesh.

clues.WINDOW: Opening with glass that gives a cabin a view of the lake
clues.SCREEN: Mesh panel fitted across a cabin window

summer-away-from-home-3.solvingTip: At 9 Down, look for the powder left after the logs burn. The crossing at 10 Across asks for what rose into the air while the logs were still burning.

notes.CHAIR: A camp chair can keep you off the ground while you listen to a story. Arranging seats in a loose circle lets people see one another around the fire.
notes.WARM: A campfire can make the side of a chair facing it feel warm. Turn the chair to another angle and you may notice how much cooler the air feels on the far side.
notes.FLAME: The flames rise above the logs and can shift as pieces of wood settle. Later, glowing coals may remain low in the fire even after the flames die down.

clues.CHAIR: One-person seat you can set beside a campfire
clues.WARM: Comfortably heated, as you may feel by a campfire
clues.FLAME: Part of the campfire that rises and flickers

summer-away-from-home-4.solvingTip: Start with what you might unfold to find the giraffes at 6 Down. The crossing at 8 Across names the walking route you would trace with your finger.

clues.VISIT: Spend time at a place, as on a trip to the zoo
clues.GATE: Entrance through which visitors pass into a zoo

notes.SHADE: At the zoo, a tree or a shelter can provide shade beside a path. Some animals also have shaded places within their enclosures.
notes.GATE: The zoo entrance gate is where visitors pass into the park. Once inside, a map can show which paths lead from there to the animal enclosures.
notes.PATH: A zoo path leads visitors from one enclosure to another. Where it splits, a sign or map can show which direction leads to the giraffes.

summer-away-from-home-5.solvingTip: Think of how far above the ground you are at the top of a Ferris wheel at 2 Across. The crossing at 1 Down asks for your trip up and around.

notes.SUMMER: At a summer fair, the Ferris wheel can run long enough to see the booths light up. The view from the top changes as the fairgrounds get darker.
notes.WHEEL: On a Ferris wheel, seats hang around the outside of the large turning circle. Each seat rises toward the top and then comes back toward the ground.

clues.WHEEL: Large turning circle that carries seats at a fair

summer-tastes-and-traditions.solvingTip: Start at 6 Down with the hard center you cut around when slicing a peach. At the crossing, 6 Across asks what the seller tells you when you ask how much.

clues.STAND: Small roadside stall that sells fresh fruit
clues.SUMMER: Season when many roadside stands sell fresh peaches

notes.SUMMER: At a roadside stand, the peach harvest often comes in during summer. Different varieties can ripen weeks apart, so the fruit on display may change between visits.
notes.FRUIT: At the peach stand, look also at the rounded shoulder near the stem. A ripe peach often has a little give there even when its red outer color varies.
notes.PRICE: A peach stand can post one price for a small basket and another for a large one. The sign's basket size tells you which amount goes with the peaches you picked up.

summer-tastes-and-traditions-2.solvingTip: Think of the frozen material packed around the cream container at 8 Down. Use the crossing at 10 Across for the handle you keep turning while the dessert freezes.

notes.HANDLE: On a hand-crank freezer, you hold the grip at the end of the crank. As you turn it, the crank drives the parts that stir the mixture inside.
notes.SUGAR: Sugar affects how the ice cream freezes as well as how it tastes. A sweetened mixture can stay softer at a temperature that would turn plain water solid.
notes.CREAM: Cream adds fat to the mixture in the hand-crank freezer. That can give the finished ice cream a smoother feel when it is scooped.

clues.HANDLE: Grip at the end of a freezer's hand crank
clues.SUGAR: Sweet ingredient stirred into homemade ice cream

summer-tastes-and-traditions-3.solvingTip: Look at one small shape on the blue part of the flag at 3 Across. Where it crosses 3 Down, picture one long red or white band beside that blue area.

notes.POLE: A porch pole holds the flag out from the wall or railing. The cloth can spread away from the pole when a breeze catches it.
notes.STAR: On the U.S. flag, each white star stands for a state. The stars are grouped against the blue corner of the flag.
notes.FLAG: The flag's stripes run across the cloth. When it hangs down without a breeze, some of those stripes can fold out of view.

clues.POLE: Support that holds a flag out from a porch
clues.STAR: White shape on the U.S. flag that stands for one state

summer-tastes-and-traditions-4.solvingTip: Find the little vessel you drink lemonade from at 4 Across. Its crossing at 3 Down asks for the slip that gets you through the fair gate.

notes.YELLOW: Plain lemonade is often pale yellow. The juice gives the drink some color, while water dilutes it.
notes.SAUCE: A sauce such as ketchup can go in a small cup beside the corn dog. That lets you dip the crisp coating one bite at a time.
notes.TICKET: Some fair booths take tickets for food. Where the fair uses that system, you hand the vendor the number posted for the corn dog or drink.

clues.SAUCE: Dip or topping you might serve with a corn dog
clues.TICKET: Paper slip exchanged for food at some fairs

summer-tastes-and-traditions-5.solvingTip: Start with what you set the finished sandwich on at 1 Across. At the crossing, 2 Down asks for the garden fruit you sliced for the filling.

notes.TOMATO: A ripe garden tomato gives the sandwich its main filling. A thick slice keeps the soft middle and firmer outer edge together in each bite.
notes.SANDWICH: A little mayonnaise on the bread helps hold the tomato slices in place. Salt and pepper can go right on the cut surfaces before the second slice of bread goes on.
notes.GARDEN: In this lunch scene, the garden is where the tomato was grown. A stake can support the vine as the fruit ripens before it is brought indoors.

clues.TOMATO: Juicy garden fruit sliced for a summer sandwich

autumn-outings-2.solvingTip: Think of the little stretch of ground full of vines at 6 Down. The crossing at 6 Across names the orange squash growing there.

clues.PATCH: Small area of ground where pumpkins grow
clues.ORANGE: Color between red and yellow on many ripe pumpkins
clues.STEM: Short stalk joining a pumpkin to its vine
clues.FALL: Season when many pumpkins finish ripening

notes.FIELD: Pumpkin vines can spread across part of a field. That smaller growing area can be called a pumpkin patch.
notes.STEM: A short stem connects the pumpkin to the long vine. That connection can dry as the squash ripens.
notes.FALL: Pumpkins often finish ripening by fall. A farm can set out different sizes after harvest so visitors can choose one for cooking or for the front step.

autumn-outings-3.solvingTip: Find what runs out as you squeeze the apples at 5 Down. Its crossing at 8 Across asks for the name of the drink made this way.

notes.HANDLE: On a screw press, turning a handle can push a plate down onto the crushed apples. The pressure releases juice that can run into a container below.
notes.JUICE: Fresh apple juice from the press can look cloudy because a little soft pulp passes through. A strainer can catch the larger bits of crushed fruit.
notes.BARREL: A barrel can hold cider after the apples have been pressed. The juice comes out of the press first and goes into a clean container for storage.

clues.HANDLE: Part you hold to turn the screw on a cider press
clues.JUICE: Liquid pressed from apples before the cider is served
clues.BARREL: Large rounded container that can hold cider

autumn-outings-4.solvingTip: At 4 Across, look for a layered bedcover you might see at the fair. Its crossing at 2 Down asks for a common four-equal-sided shape in its pattern.

notes.COLOR: A quilt maker can repeat one square shape and change the fabric colors to make a larger pattern. In a hanging display, you can often see that pattern most easily from a few steps back.
notes.RIBBON: A fair ribbon next to a quilt can mark an award. The squares and other cloth pieces sewn into the quilt make up its pattern.
notes.PATTERN: Turn a few matching quilt squares in a different direction and they can form a larger design. At a fair, you can sometimes spot both the individual squares and the larger pattern.

clues.RIBBON: Strip of cloth that can mark a fair award

autumn-outings-5.solvingTip: Find the kind of tree that grows acorns at 6 Down. Where it crosses 9 Across, picture a single piece of its fall foliage.

notes.BRANCH: From the road, the color you see comes from many leaves along each branch. Bare branches still show the shape of the tree after those leaves fall.
notes.TREE: Trees of different kinds can change color at different times in autumn. The hills can show several colors at once when you look out from the road.
notes.LEAF: A leaf can show yellow or orange as its green color fades in autumn. Other leaves may turn red, giving one stretch of road several colors.

clues.LEAF: Part of a tree that can turn red or gold in autumn

autumn-home-projects.solvingTip: Think of the heap of leaves you make in the yard at 5 Down. The crossing at 7 Across asks for one tooth on the tool used to gather it.

notes.TREE: Leaves from the same tree can land well beyond the trunk on a windy day. Raking in from the open lawn collects the scattered leaves into one pile.
notes.LEAF: A fallen leaf can curl and turn crisp as it dries on the lawn. Dry leaves can be gathered for compost, where they gradually break down.
notes.FALL: In fall, leaves can collect again under the same tree after you rake. Once they are dry, a light breeze can move them from one side of the lawn to the other.

clues.FALL: Season when many leaves drop from trees onto the lawn

autumn-home-projects-2.solvingTip: Look for one of the thick pieces of wood at 10 Across. The crossing at 4 Down names the smaller sticks you burn first to get the fire going.

notes.WINTER: The scene takes place before winter, while there is time to split and stack the logs. Keep the little starting sticks separate so they are easy to find later.
notes.WARM: Firewood in this scene is put away ready for winter. Once logs are burned indoors, the heat can help keep the room warm on a cold day.
notes.SHED: A woodshed shelters the stack from rain. Open sides can let air move around the logs as they dry.

clues.WINTER: Cold season when stacked firewood can come in handy
clues.SHED: Small building that can shelter a stack of logs

autumn-home-projects-3.solvingTip: Think of the warm fiber in the porch blanket at 5 Across. Its crossing at 4 Down describes the air that makes you reach for the blanket.

notes.PORCH: A roof can shelter the porch chair, while cool air still comes in from the sides. A folded wool blanket can lie across the chair arm until you need it.
notes.CHAIR: An armchair gives you a place to rest your elbows while the blanket covers your lap. Tucking the blanket around your knees can keep it in place in a light breeze.
notes.BLANKET: The blanket's fringe is made of loose threads along an edge. Folding that edge over the others helps keep the threads together when you put the wool cover away.

autumn-home-projects-4.solvingTip: Think of the action that opens a hard shell at 3 Down. The crossing at 8 Across asks for the tool that gives you enough pressure to do it.

notes.HANDLE: The handles on a hinged nutcracker give you leverage. Squeezing them brings the jaws together around the shell.
notes.SHELL: The hard shell gives way between the jaws of the nutcracker. The kernel is what you pick out after the loose bits of shell have fallen away.
notes.FALL: Fall is harvest time for many nuts, including walnuts. A bowl of nuts in their shells lets everyone crack a few as they want them.

autumn-home-projects-5.solvingTip: Find the papery covering on an ear of dried corn at 3 Across. At 3 Down, think of what you do to suspend the tied decoration from the door.

notes.RIBBON: Wrap a ribbon around the dry husks where they meet. Its knot can hold the ears as a group while they hang at the door.
notes.FALL: Dried ears of corn can keep their color for a fall display. Pulling the husks back reveals the kernels while leaving something to tie together.
notes.HANG: Hang the ears by the tied husks to show off the colored kernels. The loose ends of the ribbon can fall beside the ears.

clues.FALL: Season associated with a harvest corn decoration
clues.HANG: Suspend a corn decoration by its tied husks

autumn-kitchen-and-pantry.solvingTip: Find the shallow metal container you pour the batter into at 10 Across. The crossing at 6 Down asks for the squash that gives the bread its flavor.

clues.ORANGE: Color pumpkin can give a loaf of bread
clues.CINNAMON: Brown spice often used to flavor a pumpkin loaf
clues.BREAD: Kind of baked food made as a loaf with cooked pumpkin
clues.BAKE: Cook pumpkin bread in a loaf pan with oven heat

notes.CINNAMON: Ground cinnamon goes into the quick-bread batter before baking. Its warm flavor carries through the loaf so it is present in every slice.
notes.BREAD: Pumpkin bread is baked in a loaf pan and can be cut into slices when it cools. The pumpkin gives this quick bread some of its moist, cake-like texture.
notes.BAKE: Pumpkin bread bakes as one loaf in the hot oven. The heat reaches the outside first, and the center gradually sets.

autumn-kitchen-and-pantry-2.solvingTip: At 6 Across, find the part you take out to leave room for the raisins. Its crossing at 3 Down asks what you do once the filled apples go into the oven.

notes.SPOON: A small spoon can pack raisins into the opening left by the apple core. The fruit around that opening softens as it bakes.
notes.FRUIT: Both the apple and the dried grapes in the filling are fruit. The apple holds its shape like a little bowl while the raisins bake inside.
notes.CINNAMON: A pinch of cinnamon can go into the hollow left by the apple core. As the fruit heats up, its juice helps carry the spice through the filling.

clues.SPOON: Small utensil that can put raisins into a cored apple
clues.BAKE: Cook the filled apples in the oven
clues.CORE: Middle of the apple removed to make room for raisins
clues.OVEN: Heated space where the filled apples soften

autumn-kitchen-and-pantry-3.solvingTip: Think of one small block of squash cut for roasting at 8 Across. Where it crosses 6 Down, go back to the cut that divided the whole squash into two equal pieces.

clues.PEEL: Remove the outer skin from a squash
clues.SEED: Small piece scooped from the hollow inside a squash

notes.SWEET: Butternut squash has some sweetness of its own. Roasting can bring it out, especially where the cut edges begin to brown.
notes.SEED: The seeds sit in a hollow at the wide end of the squash. Once the squash is cut open, they can be scooped out with the stringy pulp.

autumn-kitchen-and-pantry-5.solvingTip: Start with the round dish that holds the roasted seeds at 7 Down. Its crossing at 10 Across asks for the hard outer covering you may find on each one.

clues.ROAST: Cook pumpkin seeds with dry heat in an oven
clues.SEED: Part scooped from a pumpkin that can be rinsed and roasted
clues.SHELL: Pale covering around the kernel of many pumpkin seeds
clues.SALT: White seasoning often sprinkled over roasted pumpkin seeds
clues.PAN: Shallow vessel that holds the seeds in the oven

notes.SEED: The hard shell surrounds the kernel of a pumpkin seed. You can roast seeds in their shells after rinsing away the pulp.
notes.SHELL: Many pumpkin seeds have a pale shell around a greener kernel. The pale edge is easy to see when you spread the seeds on the pan before roasting.
notes.SALT: Roasted pumpkin seeds can be lightly salted before they cool. Small grains are easy to scatter over the irregular shells while the seeds are spread out.

easter-spring-color.solvingTip: Think of what you briefly do with an egg over a cup of dye at 4 Down. The crossing at 4 Across describes the egg once it's ready to handle without leaving wet marks.

notes.COLOR: Dye is the liquid in the cup. Color is what you see on the shell after dipping. The shell may look lighter after it dries.
notes.YELLOW: Yellow dye can be hard to see on a brown shell. The same dye usually shows up more clearly on a white egg.
notes.EASTER: Egg decorating often comes before Easter Sunday. The dried eggs can later go into a display bowl, a basket, or an egg hunt.

easter-spring-color-2.solvingTip: Start with the outdoor area where the eggs are hidden at 3 Across. The crossing at 1 Down asks for what grows under your feet as you look for them.

clues.HIDE: Put the eggs where they are hard to see
clues.GRASS: Green lawn growth that can hide an Easter egg
clues.EASTER: Spring holiday when people may hunt for hidden eggs

notes.COLOR: Picking a range of egg colors can give an outdoor hunt some easy finds. Bright colors tend to show up well against grass.
notes.GRASS: An egg in short grass may be easy to see from the path. The same color can look more hidden among taller blades at the edge of the yard.
notes.EASTER: An Easter hunt can use decorated eggs or colorful plastic ones. A small prize can fit inside a plastic egg as a surprise for the person who finds it.

easter-spring-color-3.solvingTip: Think of one tall piece you cut out for a rabbit's head at 3 Across. Its crossing at 2 Down takes you to the small tuft you can make with cotton.

clues.TAIL: Small fluffy part at the back of a rabbit
clues.COTTON: Soft plant fiber that can make a fluffy tail on a paper bunny
clues.SCISSORS: Two-bladed tool for cutting paper bunny shapes

notes.COTTON: A small tuft of cotton makes a soft tail on the paper bunny. It also adds some depth to the otherwise flat cutout.
notes.SCISSORS: Small scissors can follow the curves around long paper ears. Turn the paper as you cut to keep the corners of the bunny shape from tearing.
notes.EASTER: A paper bunny can mark a place at an Easter table. A folded support behind the cutout can hold the ears up where they are easier to see.

easter-spring-color-4.solvingTip: Find what holds the bunch of daffodils at 7 Down. The crossing at 9 Across asks for the part of one flower that reaches down into the water.

notes.WATER: In the brunch bouquet, the cut stems draw water up from the vase. Taking off leaves below the water line keeps them from breaking down in the water.
notes.TABLE: The brunch table holds the meal and flowers. A low vase can leave guests a clear view across the table.
notes.EASTER: An Easter brunch is a spring meal between the usual breakfast and lunch hours. Daffodils are one choice for a seasonal bouquet.
